The positive pole fires on a token that completes a multi-token surface unit instead of starting a fresh word in running prose: (i) a newline that breaks the line inside a clause in hard-wrapped text (e.g. 'reviewing the\nproposal', but not a newline after sentence-final punctuation and not a line break in otherwise unwrapped prose), and (ii) the non-initial element of an uncommon multi-token word, name or label (e.g. 'sville' in Brownsville, 'stones' in brownstones, ' Mile' in Four/Seven Mile, ' Street' in Charles Street, 'content' in 'Article content'). It is near zero on ordinary word-initial content words in flowing prose, on sentence- and paragraph-final newlines, on familiar multi-token names such as New York, Main Street and Wall Street, and on the negative pole's hostile-reception frames ('come under fire'), where the same neuron is instead strongly negative.

Fires on the word naming a hostile blow, attack or (more weakly) intense attention that the sentence subject RECEIVES, read inside a patient-side frame such as 'come/be under X', 'take/taking (a lot of) X', 'get/got (a lot of) X', 'got X-ed by', 'draw/face X' (e.g. 'under fire', 'taking heat', 'took a beating/hit/knock', 'got hammered/beaten by', 'came under attack/criticism', 'got a lot of hate/love/praise'); strongest for violence/heat metaphors (beating, heat, fire, hammered, hit), weaker for criticism/attack/praise, near zero for neutral received objects (break, loss, money, review, scrutiny, funding, views). The same words used outside the receiving frame (literal 'turn up the heat', 'on fire', 'opened fire', 'beat the eggs/record') stay inactive, so the pole tracks 'subject is on the receiving end of a hit/attack', not token identity.

The pole detects the concept of an electromagnetic field/force rather than its words: it peaks on the head noun of a physics 'field' compound whose modifier names a physical force or quantity ('magnetic field' ~15, 'electric field' ~9, 'gravitational field' ~7.5, 'force field' ~4) and on the vocabulary and people of magnetism and electricity (magnet, coil, wire, flux, charge, current, induction, electromagnetic, tesla, Faraday ~4-9), in Chinese as well as English (磁场 ~13, 电磁 ~3.4). The same surface tokens in everyday senses ('football field' ~0.2, 'field of view' ~0.6, 'field of study' ~0.3, 'electric bill' ~0, 'current affairs' ~0.5, 'pole vault' ~0.1) and non-electromagnetic science (chemistry, biology, astronomy, optics ~0.2) stay near baseline, the pole is retrospective (measure_lookahead is false and peaks sit on the concept token, never one token before a fixed upcoming word), and a weaker offshoot fires on fantasy-magic force language ('magic' ~3.4, 'spell' ~4.5, 'wand' in a wizard frame ~5).

The pole is a term detector for search-engine marketing: it fires on the vocabulary webmasters and search advertisers use about a page's standing in web search - 'SEO', 'Yoast', 'search engine(s)', 'keywords', 'Pay Per Click'/'PPC', 'rank'/'ranking', 'optimise'/'optimisation'/'optimised', 'backlinks', 'SERP', 'sitemap', 'noindex', 'Googlebot', 'meta description', 'domain authority', 'Search Console', 'webmaster tools', and 'Google'/'Yahoo' named as search engines (also the equivalents in other languages, e.g. 排名/优化, 搜索引擎, posicionamiento en buscadores) - plus, more weakly, the page-head markup that carries search metadata ('meta description', 'meta robots'/'noindex', 'link rel=canonical' or 'hreflang'), and it is strongest when several such terms co-occur in one passage. The same words in other senses (a matrix's or an officer's 'rank', a missing 'link', a 'meta'-analysis, supply-chain 'optimisation', Google's corporate news), non-search advertising (television, print, email, social), generic web words ('website', 'page', 'hosting', 'stylesheet', 'browser', a plain https URL) and SEO advice reworded without these terms ('climb the results page', 'earn citations') do not fire: the trigger is the search-marketing term itself, not the general idea.

The negative pole is a graded semantic detector for temptation and enticement: it fires hardest on the word that names an allurement or impulse pulling someone toward an action they might resist or yield to — tempt/tempted/tempting/temptation (strength 5–15), urge (5–6), and entice/enticement, seduce/seductive, lure, alluring (2–7) — and, less reliably (1.5–6), on the adjacent vocabulary of yielding to or holding out against that pull (resist, give in, yield, succumb, can't help but, devil, sins, Satan); it is lexical-semantic, not propositional, so a mention fires whether the clause urges, forbids or denies the temptation ('Don't do it — this can be tempting'; 'They are tempted by nothing'). Bare function words, ordinary volition and purpose stay near zero (sentence peaks: 'I want to go' 0.42, 'He needs to go' 0.10, 'They plan to contest the ruling' 0.09, 'John and Mary travelled to Paris in spring' 0.16, 'He sat on the mat' 0.04), the propensity rim (tend, tendency, desire, inclined, attracted, appealing, craving; 0.7–2.7) is not a reliable positive, and a following 'to'/'toward' peaks only when it is the complement of one of these pull words ('we tend to', 'an urge to', 'a tendency to').

Pole N1073+ fires when a clause is anchored to an earlier time than the narrative present, and it peaks on the token that completes the framer rather than on any fixed word: the ' in' of 'back in …', the ' then'/' when' of 'back then'/'back when …', the ' of' in 'in the days of X' and 'in those/old/earlier days', the child/teen noun or its closing comma in 'when I was a little girl/teenager,' and 'when you were a kid,', the ' to' of 'used to …'/'prior to …', the ' before' of 'long before …'/'the days before …', and the ' time' of 'at the time (of)'/'at that time' (all 1.6–6.4 on the pole's 6.4 scale). Present- and future-referring counterparts of these framers fall below 0.5 ('at the moment', 'these days', 'in the coming days', 'long after us', 'is used to', '… will … in 2089'), as do non-temporal uses of the same words ('in the drawer', 'give it back', 'prior notice') and ordinary past-tense narration with no time frame ('She bought milk'); the exceptions and weak parts are that the 'when I was …' clause still gives ~2 when only its tense is made present, that numerals in past date expressions ('from 1933 to 1935', 'in 1970') give only an inconstant 0.4–2 in isolation (higher only inside an already date-rich passage), and that the 'at the/a time (of/when)' formula also fires for future or present events; the output direction promotes period/history vocabulary ('era', 'history', '年代', '岁月', 'historians'), so the pole marks a passage as set in an earlier period rather than preparing one particular next token.

The positive pole detects kinematics — a physical body's motion through space: it fires strongly when a body is projected, dropped or falling (thrown, hurled, tossed, kicked, fired, dropped, falling, 'from rest') and on kinematic quantity vocabulary (velocity, speed, acceleration, displacement, distance, height, trajectory, particle, projectile, the noun 'motion' in subject position) together with the SI units that measure motion (m, m/s, m/s2, seconds), most strongly in the setup of a mechanics word problem. It reacts retrospectively and stays inactive on the same words in figurative or non-physical use ('the game was thrown', 'prices are falling', 'the window was thrown open', 'he was fired from his job'), on plain agent-voice motion with no kinematic description ('the bird flew', 'the car moved', 'the horse galloped'), and on other sciences or non-kinematic mechanics (kinetics, a spring constant, chemistry, calculus).

The negative pole encodes the mathematical concept of a map/function between two objects: it peaks on the token that carries the correspondence - the arrow in f:X->Y ('\rightarrow', '\to', '\mapsto'), 'maps' plus its preposition ('to', 'onto', 'into'), 'from ... to' once a map or function has been named, 'between' after 'a map', and 'reversed' where a map is inverted - and on the words naming a map or its parts ('function', 'mapping', 'relation', 'range', 'inverse', 'one-to-one', 'image'), strongest when the map's arguments are abstract or symbolically denoted (X, Y, A, B, f, G, H, a vector, the kernel). The same strings outside a correspondence leave it near zero ('he climbed onto the roof', 'the train goes from X to Y', 'the bomb annihilates the city', 'a link between the two spaces', 'encryption converts the message into ciphertext'), as does mathematical prose that states no correspondence ('the polynomial has three real roots', 'the sequence converges uniformly').

Fires on words that denote the authorities taking a person into restraint, i.e. arrest, detention, custody or jail ('arrested', 'under arrest', 'into custody', 'detention'/'détention', 'sent to jail', 'caught'/'apprehended' by police, 'imprisoned'), on the illegality marker 'Unlawful/unlawful', and on the preposition right after such a verb ('arrested for', 'jailed for', 'imprisoned for'). It is weak or silent when the same word has a non-criminal sense ('joint custody', 'the ball was caught', 'in this case', 'a case of beer') and on conviction or sentencing words ('convicted', 'sentenced to', 'prison' all stay below 0.1 of max). It is retrospective: the Jacobian lens suppresses criminal/sentencing tokens rather than promoting the next token.

The negative pole fires on the penal outcome of a criminal case: the punishment a court imposes or carries out on a person and the guilt it rests on. Its strongest triggers are penalty phrases - 'sentenced/imposed/condemned to' a term ('life', 'death', 'twelve years', 'eleven months', prison, probation), 'life sentence', 'death sentence', 'death penalty', 'capital punishment', parole, the execution or lethal injection of a condemned prisoner, and the reduction or appeal of a penalty ('reduced/lessened/commuted/vacated a sentence') - together with the guilt finding ('pleaded guilty', 'plea of guilty', 'guilty verdict', 'verdict was guilty', a conviction being appealed, 'guilt', and graded serious charges such as 'first degree', 'capital', 'aggravated'). Because the trigger is the penal phrase, the same words with no penal left context ('The sentence was announced', 'Executions are carried out at dawn') stay near zero, and strength grows as several cues accumulate. It is the complement of the positive pole, which fires when the authorities take a person into restraint (arrest, custody, detention, jail, apprehension - all near zero here), and it stays near zero on crimes named without a penalty (murder, rape, fraud, burglary), on investigation and charging procedure (indictment, arraignment, prosecution, testimony, jury instructions), on civil litigation and money remedies (contract, damages, negligence, fines, restitution), and on the everyday senses of the same words ('sentence' of a paragraph, 'execution' of a plan or contract, 'life' in the ocean, 'death' of a patient, 'degree' in mathematics); a few court-room words from the legal documents it fires in ('public defender', 'defense attorney', 'assistance of counsel', 'vacate', 'handed down') reach only the low active range. Its output direction promotes this same penal lexicon rather than a specific next token, so the mechanism is retrospective.

Fires on a word naming a field of artistic, aesthetic or vernacular culture: design, art, folklore/folk, popular (as in popular culture or vote), costume, opera, sculptor, singers. It fires hardest when the word labels the whole discipline or category ('Cover design by', 'design has become', 'popular culture', 'In folklore') rather than a concrete object, and stays near zero for the same frames filled with non-cultural domains (finance, tax, medicine, price, chemistry, code). Retrospective: the peak is on the culture word itself and is driven mostly by that token and its immediate modifier.

Retrospective lexical detector for the scraped 'free download' content-farm register (greeting-card, wallpaper, quotes and font pages): activation is an additive lexical ensemble over the register's offer vocabulary - wallpapers, pictures, quotes, wishes, greetings, cards, messages, icons, downloadable, caption - plus greeting headlines ('Happy Birthday', 'Valentines Day') and design/software-asset identifiers (drawable, background, Icon, .support.constraint, FreeType, freeware, stationery), peaking on the offer-nouns themselves (peaks sit ON ' wallpapers'/' quotes'/' greetings' and the 3 following tokens are not a predictable continuation; Jacobian kurtosis 3.2, logit-lens list is noise, and Qwen2.5-0.5B's tied embeddings make the promoted ' Www'/' Wallpaper'/'Tumblr'/' Cute' list mirror the input key, so this is detection, not lookahead). Response grows with local co-occurrence density of those tokens - a bare twelve-noun register list fires 5.3 vs 0.07 for matched household nouns, a single ' wallpapers' in an otherwise mundane sentence 5.0, pure register prose up to ~12, above the corpus's diluted 3.65 max - while lone date words are a weaker offshoot the register amplifies (' day' 1.9-3.2 in mundane prose, ' Morning' 1.3 in news ratings but 6.5 inside good-morning-wishes spam), and the negative pole is the mirror contrast: it fires on encyclopedic/fan-wiki/reference text and promotes code-bracket tokens ('[$', '[arg', '”）') while suppressing exactly the ' Wallpaper'/'Tumblr' cluster.

The pole detects R-style data-analysis source code: it peaks (1.5-7, versus <=0.5 elsewhere) on the code-identifier tokens that name R functions and named arguments (c, rep, length, plot, main, col, data.frame, setCellValue, print) and on the punctuation fragments glued to them in call syntax ('(x', "('", "',", '),', ','), including the first token after a '<-' assignment. The same words in ordinary prose ('the plot of the novel', 'the mean value', or 'the c function' with no code frame), English lists, the numeric/string data values inside the code, and Java/JS method-call code stay below the activity threshold; the raw neuron is instead suppressed on the operators and delimiters that precede those identifiers ('<-', 'for', '(') and on identifier continuations ('vals', 'Row', 'CellValue'), which is the contrast its negative pole draws.

This pole is a retrospective detector for the distal demonstrative 'that'/'those' used to pick out a specific thing, set of things or proposition that the context has made available — as a pronoun ('I want that', 'with that', 'and that mattered', 'what is that?') or as a determiner ('that study', 'those findings', "That's why", sentence-initial 'That …' after a full stop or a newline) — and it is silent on the proximal 'this'/'these' and on 'that' where the preceding word already selects a complementizer or relative clause ('the fact that', 'suggests that', 'it is clear that', 'the one that I wanted'); firing is graded by how well the prefix supports that referring reading (strongest after a full stop or newline, a conjunction, a preposition or a transitive verb, weakest after nouns and clause-selecting verbs, and never at a text's very first token). It also fires more weakly and only in some contexts (roughly a tenth to a third of the demonstrative peak) on scattered specific, technical or quantitative content words — 'revenue' after 'quarterly', 'charges' after 'faced', and 'test', 'system', 'computer', 'monitor', 'processor', 'measurement', 'metric', 'unit', 'model', 'number', 'input', 'output', 'component' after a determiner — which I read as an offshoot of the same 'specific, already-identifiable referent' direction rather than a second job.

The negative pole tracks forward-looking time reference: it peaks where a clause places an event after the narrative present, either through an explicit future-time expression (' soon', ' shortly', ' imminent', ' coming', ' upcoming', ' next week/year/spring', ' in the near future', ' eventually', ' before long', ' any day now') or through a prospective predicate whose complement is still unrealized ('is set to', 'is due to', 'is expected to', 'is scheduled to/for', 'plans/intends to', 'is going to', 'is about to'). It returns to baseline when the same vocabulary describes past or completed events ('arrived soon after', 'was released in June', 'had expected to win', 'was about to leave'), present states or habituals ('leaves at six every morning'), present-tense epistemic complements ('is said/believed/reported/known to be'), and ordinary infinitival 'to' ('wants to leave'), while a bare 'will' plus a lexical verb with no explicit future-time expression is only a weak cue (typically 0.1-1.2 on the pole's 7.5 scan scale).

The negative pole fires on the token that refers to a periodical publication as an object or institution — the printed newspaper or magazine itself, not its content: strongly (about 3.5-10 of the 9.8 scale) on the periodical nouns newspaper, magazine, tabloid, broadsheet, zine, periodical, and on 'paper' in the morning-paper/newspaper sense, on their equivalents in other languages (Zeitung 6.4, periódico 8.1, quotidien 4.9, giornale 6.5, газета 6.4, 报纸 8.6) and on foreign outlet names (Le Monde 4.2, Haaretz 4.6, Le Parisien 5.8, El Diario 4.6), and, while that frame is active, on its publishing apparatus and cycle (publication/publishing/publisher 3.5-5.2, editor/editorial 3-4.7, circulation 4.3-8.5, issue, edition, 'published monthly', 'delivered twice a day', 'every week'). It stays near zero on news content and newsroom staff (news, article, headline, story, reporter, journalist, columnist, correspondent) and on broadcast/digital media (radio, television, podcast, network, blog, website), and it stays below the 0.25 x scale active threshold on common English mastheads (New York Times, Guardian ~1), on non-periodical senses of the same words (paper as material, issue as topic, press as push, journal as diary, film/photo editor, book/app/music publisher), and on journal, gazette and newsletter (~1-2.4); the peak lands on the concept-bearing token itself (often its final subword), retrospectively, and its Jacobian-lens output promotes the same publication vocabulary but does not prepare a specific upcoming token.

Pole N4792+ fires retrospectively on the technical register of evidence synthesis and appraisal: it is active on the content words of text that aggregates, grades or vouches for a body of research findings - 'systematic review(s)' (13.5-16.4 on the pole's 16.0 scale), 'meta-analysis' (15.1), 'Cochrane ... systematic reviews' (16.0), 'GRADE' with 'certainty of the evidence' (15.8), a 'PubMed/Medline search' of trials (11.6), 'quality/certainty of the evidence' (11.1), the 'eligible studies' inclusion step of a review (10.5), 'evidence-based' (6.3-7.7), a pooled or 'single estimate' aggregation over studies (6.1-7.2, and 6.4 even when the pooled items are interviews rather than studies), 'moderate evidence that ...' (6.3), 'forty-two studies of the treatment' (6.7-8.4) and 'no strong evidence that ...' (4.9), while 'peer-reviewed' (0.6-3.0), a lone 'evidence', 'review', 'studies' or 'systematic' in ordinary prose, and an isolated description of one study's design ('participants were randomly assigned to the drug or placebo in a double-blind trial', 2.6) stay at 0.4-4.8. It does not fire on the same words in other senses (film/performance review <=0.23, a criminal trial <=0.29, pooled funds 0.00, evidence in court <=0.18), on generic science statements ('research shows', 'scientists discovered', 'Science has shown' <=0.6), or on plain-language paraphrases without the technical terms ('a careful summary of many experiments ... moderately confident' <=3.5); it is topic-independent - the same phrases reach 15-19 in astronomy, education, business and machine-learning text - and ablating the pole removes probability from the same register words ('review', 'systematic', 'meta', 'evidence', 'research', 'study') rather than from one particular upcoming token, so the claim is retrospective.

This pole fires retrospectively on the token that completes a lexicalized multi-token chunk: a subword piece finishing a split (usually technical or rare) word (Richt+er, seism+icity, megaw+att, pre+term, myd+ri+asis, Apog+ee, f+ission, cord+ite, norm+ative, U++) or the second word of a fixed collocation (Family+planning, low+fertility, sea+ice, seismic+waves, domestic+energy, X+-linked), i.e. when the current token is strongly cued by the immediately preceding 1-2 tokens. Near-miss: the identical tail token after a non-cueing prefix (careful+planning 0.02, sea+spray, Family+dinner) or the same stem as a merged single token stays near zero; acknowledged leftovers are a weak transit-noun offshoot (station/platform ~0.5, amplified by rail-topic long context) and the scan's generic we+can peak, which does not replicate in isolation.

The negative pole detects the head of a clause-level circumstance adjunct from a small set — 'with', 'once' and the compound 'now that' — firing where that head is complete: on 'with' when it sits at a clause's left edge (sentence-initial after a full stop, newline or semicolon, or after a coordinator such as 'and'/'but' or the complementizer 'that'), on 'once' when it heads a clause (fronted or trailing, including sentence-initial idioms like 'Once again'), and on the 'that' of clause-initial 'now that'. The same words inside a clause are near zero — 'with' as a verb complement, NP-internal modifier, postposed or parenthetical with-phrase; 'once' as a clause-internal frequency adverb — as are other clause-initial prepositions and subordinators (in, at, by, for, after, when, if, because, although, while), which stay below the active threshold.

Retrospective detector for noun phrases naming support roles, service departments, facilities, or equipment that an institution provides to its members (e.g. chaplains, counsellors, financial-aid advisors, Human Resources, washrooms, meals, busses, generators, radios), typically peaking at the completion of the compound; strength is boosted when the surrounding passage describes the institution providing, inspecting, or maintaining them, consistent with its staff/logistics output direction and heavy long-range attribution.

The positive pole fires on sentences that narrate a particular person's life: life-event and relationship wording (born, married, died, survived, joined, attended, worked, convicted) together with kin/role nouns (wife, husband, son, daughter, father, mother, children, family, Dr, professor, poet, mayor) predicated of an individual referred to by a personal name or by a singular person pronoun (he/she/his/her/him, I/my/me). It stays near zero on impersonal prose about materials, reactions, algorithms, committees, products or code, and on plural, collective or inanimate reference (they/their, we/our, it/its), e.g. 'the idea was born out of a merger' or 'the company said it would acquire the firm' do not fire while 'his wife published the collection' and 'she married a local merchant' do.

Fires on the token that commits a clause to putting forward something for others to accept or act on: the verb (its final subword) of demand/request/proposal/imposition verbs whose object is the content sought or proposed rather than a person (dictate, demand, request(ed), recommend, advocate, prescribe, propose, suggest, impose, submit, French 'ordonné'), the particle 'for' in 'asked/begged/called for', 'out' after verbs of calling out (yell/holler/call out), and 'Submitted:' in court-opinion headers; weaker (about a third to a half of max) on content-delivering verbs (mention, explain, clarify, contribute). It is near-silent on verbs of wanting or needing (want, need, require), deciding or handling (approve, reject, review, discuss, receive, get), giving (offer, provide, give), non-request 'for' (looked/waited/paid for), and person-object frames ('asked them', 'begged them', 'urged them'), which instead drive the negative pole; together the two poles split communicative verbs into 'acting on a person's mind' (negative) versus 'putting forward a demand or proposal' (positive).

Fires on the verb token itself (its final subword) of transitive verbs whose direct object is a person whose knowledge, belief or holdings the subject changes: informing/reminding/warning/advising/alerting/telling, persuading/convincing/reassuring/begging, thanking/congratulating/accusing, and robbing/depriving (e.g. ' reminding', ' persuade', ' informing', ' convince', ' thank', ' rob', 'ive' in 'deprive'); strongest for the progressive or bare form after an auxiliary or connective ('is reminding', 'had to persuade', 'without first informing'). It is weak or silent on transitive verbs that act on a person without altering what they know or have (help, force, sway, bring, show, greet, praise, blame, allow), on the object and complement that follow, and on noun or adjective derivatives ('reminder', 'information', 'informed consent', 'persuasive').

Fires (retrospectively) on the token where someone's turn or response in an exchange is introduced or named: most strongly the opening quotation mark or colon that begins a quoted utterance right after a speech-act tag ("interrupted, “", "continued:", "interjected, “"), then reply/speech-act verbs in dialogue tags (answered, replied, insisted, suggested, asked, demanded; not non-speech tags like nodded, smiled, sighed) and nouns naming a chosen strategic response (move, switch, pick, choice, action, response, reply, counsel/defense), but not plain nouns like bill, plan, idea, trip or hire. A separate strong token-level offshoot: 'dominant' (and weaker 'recessive') as a mode of genetic inheritance ("autosomal dominant", "the gene is dominant"), plus 'no matter what'.

The pole fires on tokens that belong to the name of a specific, real-world legal or institutional instrument in formal/reference prose: the title word of a statute or constitutional amendment ('Act', 'Amendments', 'Terms'), the words of a treaty, convention or protocol name ('Kyoto Protocol', 'Basel Convention', 'Treaty of Versailles', 'European Convention on Human Rights', 'ILO Convention 128'), and the party names and 'v.' of a case citation ('Drummond v. Commissioner', 'Smith v. Jones'); a weaker offshoot of the same response appears on other recognised encyclopedic designations ('Athens', 'the Bristol Stool Score', 'Pusan International Forum', '802.3at', 'September 11'). It stays near baseline in ordinary lowercase running text, on the same place or party words when they are not naming an instrument or designation (casual talk, weather, travel, invented names such as 'Zorb Protocol'), and on bare country or person names.

The negative pole fires on a word asserting that a thing, property or quantity is absent or zero: the negative determiner 'no' in a predicate noun phrase ('there is/are/was/were no X', 'has/had no X', 'with no X', 'found/showed/contains no X'), zero-value words ('null', 'undefined', 'None', 'none', 'nil', 'zero', 'Off'), zero-price 'free', privative words ('-less', 'unavailable', 'absent', 'omitted', 'extinct', 'missing', 'lack', 'without', 'devoid', 'waived', 'exempt') and negated existence ('does not exist', 'if (!x)'), reaching 0.8-3.5 (up to 5.2 on 'waived') against the 1.06 active threshold (0.25 x the scan max of 4.23). It is not sentential negation or a generic negative-polarity detector: 'not', 'never' and "don't" stay at or below about 0.5, as do the discourse answer 'No.', 'No.' meaning 'number', container-state 'empty'/'blank'/'full', sentence-initial 'No X' subjects, and every affirmative counterpart ('there is some water', 'the fee is charged').

Fires retrospectively on words denoting internal operational components or organs of physical devices and anatomical systems (such as mechanical/electrical working parts like alternator, filament, fuse, relay, piston, pump, and visceral organs like kidney, stomach, colon), as well as thermodynamic phase changes (e.g., boils) and expressions of capacity or inability (e.g., can't, cannot). It remains inactive on external body parts, everyday furniture, abstract concepts, and non-capacity modal verbs.

Fires on the word that says a just-mentioned cause, tool or action makes some outcome possible: enabling verbs used causatively ('enable(s)/enabling', 'allow(s)/allowing', 'permit(s)', 'let(s)', 'help(s)', 'facilitate', French 'permettre'), the means connective 'That/This way', 'makes it possible', and purpose 'to' after a means ('use cookies to'). It stays near zero on non-enabling verbs in the same slot (improve, prevent, require, force), on nominal or imperative uses ('the permit', 'Allow me'), and on literal 'way' ('the long way home').

Fires on the OPENING delimiter of an inline markup span in prose or scientific text, i.e. the token that starts a Markdown/Pandoc formatted run glued to the following word: Pandoc subscript/superscript '~' and '^' (as in T~2~, (SurfO)~2~, 2^nd^), Markdown emphasis ' *' / ' _', fused italic tokens like '_N', '_O', '_the', and Apex '__' in '__c'; the matching closing delimiter stays near zero, the same characters used as ordinary punctuation or code identifiers (my_var, H_2O, -, =) do not fire, and activation is much stronger when the document has already used that kind of inline markup earlier (the second '~'/'^'/'_' opener beats the first, and bare ' _' italics barely fire without prior markup). Weaker leftovers (~0.3 of max) are other span-opening punctuation such as opening quotes, parenthetical dashes ' –', ' /' in '/CNW/' and a dateline comma.

Retrospective detector for feminine reference at or just after the current token: it fires when the peak token itself is a feminine-marked word (pronoun she/her/herself, female proper name such as Marie, feminine role noun such as princess/girls/women) or the word immediately continuing a feminine-subject clause; masculine counterparts and gender-neutral words stay near baseline.

This pole fires retrospectively when the current token completes a binary paired frame opened within the previous ~6 tokens: a from->to range endpoint, a change-of-state verb->into complement, or the separator/second item of a two-element formal pair (numeric tuple, column list, argument list, coordinator), with weaker firing on determiner->noun and similar head-complement completions. The same token stays near-silent without its opener (purpose-'to', 'into' after a non-conversion verb, comma outside a pair), and swapping the frame's content leaves firing unchanged.

The pole fires on an emphatic anaphoric demonstrative - 'that' used as pronoun or determiner, 'this', 'those', or the free relative 'what' - when it picks out a specific entity, action, kind, reason or degree already given in the preceding text and is focused by an immediately preceding focus particle ('just', 'exactly', 'precisely', 'only', 'simply', 'literally', 'even'), as in 'did exactly that', 'for precisely that reason', 'exactly what I need', 'just that kind of afternoon'; the peak sits on the demonstrative itself. It is a demonstrative-reference detector, not an exactness or 'that'-token detector: the same frame falls four- to ten-fold, to or below the activity line, when the demonstrative becomes the article or a plain pronoun ('exactly the reason', 'exactly the kind', 'precisely it'), when the focus particle is deleted ('did that', 'what she needed') or replaced by a non-focus adverb ('certainly that reason'), and when 'that' is a complementizer or cleft expletive ('said that he would', 'then that the train') or 'what' is interrogative rather than a free relative ('know exactly what she needed').

The pole fires at a preposition ('by', 'of', 'with', 'from', sometimes 'to') or at the determiner immediately after it, when the preceding predicate or noun sets up a person-involving relation: authorship, ownership, provenance or social interaction ('written', 'produced', 'built', 'owned' + 'by'; 'spoke', 'talked', 'met' + 'with'; 'heard' + 'from') or a person's attribute or experience ('the lives of', 'the voices of', 'the eyes of', 'the attention of', 'on behalf of'). It does not fire when the same prepositions relate things rather than people - physical manipulation, destruction or consumption ('destroyed by', 'washed by', 'eaten by', 'cut with'), part/whole or object possession ('the roof of', 'the cover of'), spatial or temporal location ('sat on', 'in the city', 'at noon') - nor on compound prepositions ('because of', 'according to').

Retrospectively detects references to a named, versioned artifact (software, spec, publication, hardware, or event edition), peaking on the release noun itself (version, edition, firmware, software, kernel) or on the digit/decimal suffix completing the identifier (e.g. version 1.5, Rails 3.0, MathML2, B12, Mach 2.04, Ninth Edition); identical digits after generic nouns (year 2016, price 2.04, dinner 1.5) stay near zero.

The positive pole detects the speaker/writer's own deictic self-reference: it fires on the first-person pronoun tokens ' I', 'I', ' me', ' my', 'My', ' we', 'We', ' us', ' our', 'Our' (with first-person contractions such as 'm/'ll/'ve and cross-lingual equivalents 'nous', 'notre', 'mi', 'Vi'), and sits at its floor on second- and third-person pronouns (you/he/him/his/they/them/their, 0.0-0.5 in the same frames) and on 'I' inside a technical identifier (IGF-I, I2C, IIC, at or below 0). Within first-person pronouns the strength separates an utterance put to a hearer from narration: appeals, apologies, corrections, self-justifying questions and quoted dialogue clear the activity line ('forgive me for...' 6.06, 'correct me if I...' 6.37, 'don't get me wrong' 3.66, 'What did I do wrong?' 4.72, 'the trouble I have caused you' 3.50, 'Do we know you at all?' 2.76, against 2.87 / 2.86 / 0.50 / 0.43 / 0.15 / 0.10 when only the pronoun's person changes; the bare 'forgive X for' and 'correct X if' frames keep a residual near 2.9 whatever the person), whereas first-person pronouns in plain third-person narration stay far below it ('the meeting ended early, and I walked home alone' 0.88, 'the report said that I had missed the deadline' 0.94).

The pole fires on a hand-held implement - a tool, weapon, musical instrument, eating or writing implement, or portable device - presented as an object in a person's hands: it peaks on the implement noun itself (chisel, hammer, rifle, camera, knife, guitar, wrench), is strongest with grip and manipulation verbs (grip, swing, pick up, carry, raise, clean, holster) and weakest when the same noun is only mentioned, owned or banned. It falls to baseline for non-implement graspables in identical frames (food, rope, stones, boxes, clothing), furniture and abstract nouns, stays sub-threshold for vehicles and machines even when operated, and fires at roughly half strength on the third-person possessive that introduces a handled object ('picked up his ...', 'raising his/her ...') even when that object is not an implement.

Retrospective: the pole fires at the onset of a main clause that resumes after a fronted dependent element (a participial phrase, prepositional phrase, if/when-clause or appositive) that closes just before the peak, usually at a comma but often without one, and it peaks on the resumed clause's opening auxiliary/modal/wh-word or subject pronoun (' could', ' would', ' can', ' may', ' what', ' who', ' is', ' I', ' we', ' has', "'ve") or its first predicate word (' possible', ' suggest', ' critical'); the fronted element can be as short as two tokens and long prefaces neither help nor hurt (measured delta -0.02), so the pole is not context-length dependent. Firing is strongest when the resumed clause is a question, request, suggestion, or possibility/obligation/evaluation statement ('could you please', 'is it possible to', 'I suggest', 'it is critical that'); the same tokens continuing rather than resuming a clause (embedded 'what', mid-clause 'would', object 'I'), coordination and serial-list commas, sentence-starting clauses with no fronted element, and code/escape text all stay near zero, and the Jacobian lens is flat (kurtosis 3.5, agreement 0%) with a suppressed list of backslash/escape tokens that exactly mirrors the negative pole's promoted list, so this is a prose clause-resumption feature, not a lookahead or code-region unit.

Fires on an adverbial means/manner/circumstance preposition attached to a preceding verb phrase ('with', 'by', 'through', 'using', 'via'; e.g. 'lowball me with', 'outscored all opponents by', 'woke me with', 'mitigated through', sentence-initial 'By using/By payment') and peaks on that preposition or on the first token of its object (usually the determiner/possessive 'a/an/their/his', a number, or a gerund). It stays near zero for the same words in other roles (comitative 'came with a friend', noun-modifying 'the woman with a red hat', passive agent 'written by a famous author') and for non-means prepositions in the same slot ('about', 'for', 'of', 'in', 'at', 'after'). A separate leftover: it also fires strongly on the token ')\n' that closes a legal citation year like '646 (2001)' followed directly by a newline.

The negative pole fires on the function word at which a partitive quantity phrase hands over to the definite thing being measured: ' of' when it follows a numeral, an indefinite quantifier or a quantity/realisation noun ('two of the drives', '13 of the drives', 'several of the drivers', 'an older version of the driver', 'a sample of the mixture'), and, most strongly, the ' the' that follows such an ' of' when the head is a substance-amount noun (concentration, amount, quantity, volume, sample, presence, mixture, solution, mass - e.g. 'a high concentration of the powder', 'a large amount of the liquid', 'the presence of the tumour'). It is near zero on the same two tokens everywhere else: after property or ratio nouns ('the colour / temperature / name / purpose / position of the powder', 'a large proportion / fraction / share / part of the powder'), after definite-set quantifiers ('most / all / half / none of the'), and on ' the' in ordinary definite noun phrases ('store the drives in the cabinet', 'the first', 'the most').

This pole detects formulaic, stored text rather than composed prose: it peaks on the token where a memorized or repeated formula is recognised - the opening tokens of successive items of a packed QA/math-dataset list ('What is the greatest common divisor of', 'Calculate', 'Is', 'Does'), the attribution line of a licence/copyright header ('...and contributors.', 'The Chromium Authors'), and a small set of stock web strings ('We use cookies', 'You can unsubscribe at any time', 'Please enter your...'). It stays inactive for the same words in ordinary sentences and one-off questions, and for generic boilerplate that lacks those exact formulas ('All rights reserved', 'Powered by WordPress').

Retrospective detector of a stated age of a particular person: it peaks on the token that completes the age phrase - 'old' in 'N-year-old' or 'N years old', the numeral of 'aged N' / 'at age N', and the digits of a bare appositive age ('Name, 60,'). It stays near zero when the same forms describe a non-person or are generic ('the tree was 56 years old', 'men aged 44', '56-page', 'at mile 80'); a weaker (0.5-2) response also occurs on the 'of/from <place or institution>' appositive that identifies a named person ('First Last, of Springfield').

This pole fires when the current token continues an already-open phrase or clause (determiner/adjective to noun, noun to complement or preposition, verb to complement or adverb, stem to suffix, number to unit, keyword to identifier), with strength boosted by a longer same-clause preamble; it stays near zero on tokens that open a new constituent (sentence-initial words, finite main verbs after subjects) and on boundaries such as '.' and 'not', even for otherwise-activating tokens.

The pole fires on a human or institutional reference that is a party to a relation or attribution rather than a bare topic: the object or complement of a contact, speech, meeting or reporting verb or preposition ('interviewed the engineer', 'spoke with the pilot', 'quoted the nurse', 'According to a source close to the family'), or a role/title/kinship reference being introduced or identified together with a name or description ('said co-author Jeff MacInnes', 'lead researcher Benjamin Lok', 'the nurse, a former colleague', 'the author of the study'). It stays inactive when the same person noun is a plain subject/agent or predicate nominal of a simple clause ('The engineer arrived', 'She is a doctor'), when the person is only the topic of a statement or management verb ('described/praised/hired the engineer'), and when the phrase is a bare role noun with a generic place or group complement ('the mayor of the city arrived', 'a member of the committee said').

The pole fires where a clause says that a valued, needed thing is absent, denied, insufficient or being cut down, and peaks on that valued word or on the operator's complement: a negator or a reduction/removal word (no, not, without, cannot, lack of, not enough, less, little, insufficient, reduce, cut, lower, block, limit, restrict, minimize, deny) applied to a benefit, right, resource or capacity such as safety, water, jobs, rights, pay, health, freedom, prosperity, quality, motivation or absorption. It stays quiet when the same negator or reduction word applies to something unwanted ('reduce crime/poverty/costs/risks', 'no problems', 'not dangerous'), when the same valued noun sits under a neutral or supportive verb ('describe/measure/improve/protect the quality', 'increases prosperity'), and on bare intransitive decline ('profits fell').

The positive pole is a retrospective detector for the relator of a transfer-or-subjection predication in formal prose: it fires on the verb that puts a theme through a process, into a new state, or under an authority ('assigned' 1.31, 'randomized' 1.59, 'subjected' 0.85, 'underwent' 0.98, 'transferred' 0.65, 'converted' 0.60, 'tested' 0.50, 'distributed' 0.49, 'undergo' 1.52; everyday manipulation verbs stay down - 'washed' 0.09, 'measured' 0.09, 'counted' 0.04) and, more strongly, on the directional preposition that introduces that predicate's goal, regime or medium ('to' 2.41 in 'assign the samples to groups', 'into' 1.02 in 'transformed the data into insights', 'under' 1.15 in 'distributed under the license', 'through' 1.42 in 'pass it through a hash', Spanish 'en' 1.71 in 'convertir ... en un valor primitivo'). It sits at the floor when those same prepositions are infinitival, static or agentive ('I want to go home' 0.00, 'walk into the room' 0.01, 'the cat is under the table' 0.15, 'assign the samples in groups' 0.54 versus 'to groups' 2.41), so neither the token nor the preposition alone carries it; the negative pole is far sparser (84 versus 498 tokens above a quarter of its max) and peaks on static-description predicates ('define' 2.55, 'surrounds' 1.96, 'includes' 1.02), which I read as the complementary sense but have not audited separately.

The pole fires on the predicate of a plain declarative clause that has a direct object, peaking on the finite lexical verb and again one token later on the determiner that opens its object, when the clause's subject denotes a concrete, non-agentive thing: a natural material or substance (rock, granite, coal, mineral, salt, iron, clay, sand, soil, sediment, water, ice, oil), a plant or plant part, or a generic physical object such as 'things' or 'an object' ('The rock removes the minerals from the soil'; 'an object that surrounds the primitive type'). It stays near-silent on the same predicate when the subject is an agent or an abstraction - an occupational or institutional role (doctor, nurse, driver, manager), an organisation or policy (company, government, rule), a manufactured device (machine, system, program) or an idea or theory - and it is also silent on the subject noun itself, on intransitive or copular predicates ('The granite erodes quite slowly', 'The granite is common') and on light verbs (use, take, require, store, support).

The negative pole fires, retrospectively, on the token that completes a memorised multi-token string belonging to a technical artefact: the second element of a fixed legal/technical expression ('notice of', 'Request for', 'CHANGE MASTER', 'Chem. Eur.', 'further notice') or of a known identifier or log label ('com.intellij.openapi.vfs.Virtual|File', 'Page|Reference', 'Job|Context', 'debug1:'), i.e. the position where one or two left-hand tokens plus a stored string already fix the token's identity. It is not a syntax, register or next-token-probability detector: the identical surface token elsewhere is silent (' of' occurs 3,422 times in the scan and exceeds 0.5 only three times, all 'notice/notified of'; 'Content-Type:', 'SQLSTATE', 'Fatal Protocol Error' and 'House of Representatives' stay under 0.25), while swapping the anchor word ('notice'->'note', 'Request'->'demand', 'debug1'->'Debug1', 'Chem. Eur.'->'Chem. Biol.', 'JobContext'->'ItemBucket') or the identifier's memorised prefix sharply reduces the response (2.21->0.12, 1.94->0.30, 1.75->0.12, 1.42->0.22, 1.65->0.73, 1.15->0.55).

The negative pole reacts retrospectively to a setting/frame phrase: it fires on the noun that names the region, span, state or dimension within which a statement is situated (time, period/era/date/interval/age, distance, elevation, temperature, pressure, price/cost, size, position/place, conditions/terms, presence/absence, groups/categories, units such as gram, inch, revolution), when that noun is the complement of a locative or scope preposition (in, at, under, during, throughout, within, inside, over, across, among, between, per), and on the 'of' (or 'per') that binds such a parameter to its value. It stays at baseline for the same nouns under non-locative prepositions (before, after, since, through, with, about, regarding, despite), for the same nouns with no governing preposition, and for concrete nouns in the same slots ('at the house', 'the colour of the sky'); scattered weaker fires on code and LaTeX values (after '=', ':', '/', inside brackets) are not explained by this claim.

This pole is a subject-verb number-agreement detector: it fires on the token carrying a third-person-singular form - a 3sg finite verb (is, was, has, does, or -s forms such as works, explains, drops) or the 3sg possessive 'its' - when that form's grammatical subject/antecedent is plural, including across intervening material or a relative pronoun ('The keys to the cabinet is' peaks at 'is' while 'The key to the cabinets is' does not; irregular plurals such as children/mice/women and invariant nouns the model represents as plural, such as fish/sheep/police, also fire). It stays inactive when the singular form agrees with a singular subject, when the verb is plural/past/bare after a plural subject, when the singular form is inverted before its subject, and when a plural noun is only a nearby non-subject; a plural verb with a singular subject ('The cat are outside') does not fire either, because the 3sg-marked form is required.

The positive pole fires on a plural noun that names something each member of a set possesses or exhibits individually - the distributive-possession reading: personal attributes and belongings ('their homes', 'very harsh childhoods', 'criminal pasts', 'their bags/coats/lunches', 'the heads of the patient') and per-item properties ('the sizes of the images', 'brief histories of the properties', fluorescence 'intensities'). It peaks on the plural noun itself (or on its plural suffix token when BPE splits the word, e.g. 'hometown'+'s' at 3.99), is boosted when a plural possessor scopes the noun ('their/our/children's + plural noun', 'the Xs of the Ys', and the distributive markers 'own' and 'themselves'), and falls to near zero (0.03-0.7) on the singular of the same noun, on plurals of generic objects in unpossessed position ('the chairs', 'tables', 'boxes', 'trucks'), on plural person nouns ('parents', 'teachers', 'students'), on irregular plurals used as plain subjects ('children', 'people', 'men'), and on singular nouns that merely end in -s ('bus', 'glass', 'analysis'). The negative pole stays near zero on the same inputs, and the transported output direction promotes the plural/distributive pronouns and quantifiers ('Their', 'their', '各自', '各', '他们的') that are the vocabulary of this feature.

The pole fires, retrospectively, on the joint where a stance predicate hands over to the material it governs: the complement or reason marker that follows a predicate of desire, ability, necessity or feeling ('wanted to', 'would like to', 'had to', 'able/unable to', 'hard/difficult to', 'due to', 'hoped for', 'delighted/glad/excited to', 'frustrated/sad/bummed because', 'since'), and the predicate token itself, with past-tense, reported forms much stronger than present-tense ones ('I wanted to' 0.99 at ' wanted' versus 0.29 for 'I want to'). The same joint fires inside formulaic records whose next value is fixed by convention rather than composed - the page number of a reporter citation ('472 U.S. 511'), the next field of a timestamp ('08:28:43'), a stack frame's '<module>' - while plain narration of events and generic description ('I wrote a new worship song', 'the cat sat on the mat') stay at zero.

The negative pole fires while a fixed, formatted element of a document is being completed: on the run of '=' that underlines a one-word section title ('Introduction
====', 'Abstract
====', 'Methods
===='), on the first token of the line that follows a 'To:'/'cc:' email-header block (normally the next field name, 'Subject'), on a forum answer's opening word immediately after the 'A:' marker ('So', 'First', 'Correct'), on a legal caption's party-role word ('Plaintiff-Appellee'), and on 'Content-Type' inside a 'http-equiv="..."' meta tag; a schema's own field word also fires when the same sentence names the schema ('the email subject'). It stays near zero on those words in ordinary narrative prose, on ordinary sentence-initial words, on markdown '#' headings and bullets, on code keywords, tags and punctuation, on hard-wrapped line breaks, and on header blocks made only of 'From:'/'Date:' lines.

N917+ fires, retrospectively, on the token where text stops being written as an ordinary word and is instead spelled out piece by piece by a surface convention: the digit that opens a group inside a formatted numeral ('more than 20,|0|00 artifacts' 0.89, versus 0.23 for '20000' in the same sentence), the non-initial piece of a hyphenated or locant technical compound ('at' in 'HIV-|patients' 0.84 against 0.13 for 'HIV patients'; 'im' in '5,6-di|methylpyrazine' 0.33), or a piece of a long dotted/slashed or boilerplate string ('.lua' inside a 22-token fontloader package path 0.41; ' License' in 'Apache License, Version 2.0' 0.39 but 0.07 in 'License plates'). The peak is the first token of that spelled-out run, the rest of the run carries a decaying tail (0.89 -> 0.49 -> 0.00 across '20,000'), and the same surface token written as a plain word, plus ordinary prose, stays near the ~0.07 background.

The negative pole is a sparse rare-name reader: it peaks on a single piece of an uncommon, non-compositional lexical item - a capitalised name the tokenizer splits into several pieces (Jodrell 'rell' 0.81, Merian 'ian' 0.82, Cocos 'ocos' 0.62, Antikythera 'ther' 0.68, Rahmstorf 'm' 0.96 with 'orf' 0.30, Zwicky 'icky' 0.50), an acronym or code (JPL 'PL' 0.83, PROBA-V 'BA' 0.56, ALOS 'LOS' 0.46, GLP-1 'P' 0.71) or a digit/hyphen string (10.3389 '9' 1.14, '-0700' '7' 0.68, 41.73N 'N' 0.67), while ordinary words and familiar single-token names stay at background (Dickens 0.06, London 0.00, Smith 0.04) and the same piece token stays silent inside a common word ('rell' 0.81 in Jodrell but 0.00 in Morrell), so the trigger is the whole rare word being spelled out, not the piece. The detector is graded and word-specific - on a fresh 500-document pass of the scan corpus a multi-piece capitalised word reached 0.4 in 1.16% of its occurrences versus 0.02% for single-token lowercase tokens, yet only ~1% of such words fire and many rare names stay silent (Wolverhampton 0.06, Kidderminster 0.10, Grangemouth 0.06) - and it is neither a surprisal nor a position detector (peak tokens are forced completions with surprisal ~0 and rho = -0.07 against surprisal; position r2 = 0.004), with an incoherent promoted-token set (Jacobian kurtosis 3.5, logit/Jacobian overlap 0) and a zero-ablation KL of 1.3e-4 on peak prompts, so the claim is retrospective.

The pole fires on a common noun, or the classifying/relational adjective built from one, that names a broad class or domain at the superordinate (kind) level - category words such as sports, sport, sporting, animal, fruit, mammals, plants, metal, aircraft, awards, mathematics, music and religious - when the word is labelling the class itself: as the modifier of a classifying compound ('a sports journalist', 'animal husbandry', 'social media', 'religious fervor'), as the plural or generic name of a class ('... and other animals', 'the four fundamental forces of nature', 'numerous awards and nominations'), or as a topic mention ('In mathematics, ...'); the surrounding passage does not have to be in that domain. It stays at the floor for a word that names a specific member of such a class or a particular object (football, dog, apple, jet, chair, jazz, algebra), for proper names, numbers and function words, and for a class word inside an unrelated fixed compound or named body ('a cell phone', 'the League of Nations').

The pole fires on a preposition (mostly ' at' or ' on', also ' for', ' as' (and the article after it), ' under', ' by') that opens a second, different-role adjunct of the clause directly after a finished PP of place, population or audience whose object is a closed referent: a 'City, Region' name pair ('He died in Portland, Oregon at age 71' 1.22, 'born in Monterrey, Mexico on 12 May' 1.11, 'met his wife in Dublin, Ireland at a wedding' 1.03), a 'for <people> with <condition>' description followed by a street address ('a hostel for teenagers with mental health problems at 41 Station Road' 1.59, 'a shelter for men with ... problems at 149 W.' 2.4), a coordinated group of test subjects ('tested in dogs and monkeys for heart toxicity' 1.08) or web pages ('cookies record your activity on our websites for marketing purposes' 1.80); a name pair, coordination or parenthetical in that closed PP multiplies strength 2-8x over a bare common noun ('died in the quiet house at age 71' 0.15, 'tested in the laboratory for' 0.24). It stays below ~0.4 when the same preposition comes straight after the verb or its direct object (so moving the adjunct before the place PP kills it: 'died at age 71 in Portland, Oregon' 0.41 on the later ' in'; 'tested for heart toxicity in dogs' 0.12), after a PP whose object is a bare common noun, on ordinary noun-modifying PP chains ('the Gulf of Mexico', 'the shore of the lake', 'through the sealed port under', all < 0.2), after verbs like 'looked at', and when the closed name ends the sentence ('He moved to Denver, Colorado.' 0.14); ' in <year>' after a name pair is weaker (0.2-0.8) than ' at'/' on'.

The negative pole fires retrospectively on clauses describing the mental retrieval, recollection, or forgetting of past information (e.g., 'remember', 'recall', 'forgot'), as well as idiomatic expressions describing the passage or elapsing of time (e.g., 'went by', 'time flies', 'passed since'). It remains inactive on physical motion, non-recollective cognitive states (such as knowing or perceiving), and identical function words in non-temporal or non-memory contexts.

Fires when the text talks about the complement of a set that is already on the table - how much else there is besides the item just named. Strongest on exclusion/addition connectives aimed outside the mentioned item ('apart from / aside from / other than / besides / except for / beyond that/this/X,', peaking on the anaphor or on the comma that closes the phrase), on negative-polarity remainder quantifiers ('no other', 'nothing/little else', 'nothing/little more', 'no further', 'nothing besides'), and on exhaustiveness predicates ('that's / that is it/all', 'that's not all', 'X is all you need/said/have'); it stays inactive where the same words name no set - spatial 'apart/aside/beyond/next', positive 'other/else/more' ('other people', 'much else', 'more questions'), bare exclusives ('the rest', 'the last', 'sole', 'complete'), and other connectives ('because of that', 'before that', 'despite that', 'moreover', 'in addition').

The pole detects the stock 'more information / ask us / get in touch' formulae of written prose and peaks on their cue words: 'more'/'further' inside a purpose phrase ('For more information/details, ...' or '... for more details'), 'any' in 'if you have/need any ...', 'to' in 'do not hesitate to ...', and 'about'/'concerning'/'regarding'/'on' linking 'questions' to its topic. It does not fire on the bare directive itself ('Contact us', 'Visit our website', 'Click here'), on the same words in argument position ('she asked for more information', 'he did not hesitate to contact me'), or on ordinary conditionals ('if it rains'); because the peak is at the cue word, a fronted 'For more ...' is already active even when the continuation turns out not to be informational ('For more than twenty years').

Fires where a formatted document steps back out to a shallower structural level after content: the leading whitespace plus delimiter of a line that dedents relative to the line above it in code, markup or data (a dedented line fires ~2.0 whether it closes a tag or opens one, while the same line at the same indentation without the dedent fires ~0.5; strength grows with depth, nested JSON/HTML at depth 1->4 giving ~0.8->~4.4), and in prose documents the line-initial section index that resumes a numbering scheme after the previous section's body ('2.'/'II.' after a '1.'/'I.' section: 3.8 with the earlier index and a body, 0.9 without it). It is near zero in flat prose, at same-level or indent-increasing lines, and at confident but non-structural continuations.

This pole fires on degree/comparison phrasing that qualifies how strongly a property holds: a degree modifier with a gradable head ('too'/'a little'/'a bit' + adjective, adverb or quantifier - 'a little too neat', 'a few too many', 'too much for them', 'too deeply ingrained'; adjectival 'enough'; the 'the X-er the Y-er' correlative), with the peak on the modifier, on its head, or - highest - on the function word that opens the phrase's complement ('to'/'be' in 'too long to be sent', 'for' in 'too neat for my taste', 'to' in 'general enough to treat'). It also fires on 'if' conditionals (peak on the following subject/copula, as in 'if something is ...'), on hedged modals ('seems like it ought to ...') and on the newswire byline 'Name (@handle)' at its closing parenthesis, whereas plain factual predication and bare intensifiers ('The book is neat', 'The book is very neat') leave it near zero.

The pole fires on a mention of the counterpart of a party already established in the passage: the second or other member of a named pair ("another material" after one material, "a second material", "the other material"), the second of two compared or contrasted parties ("For men" after women, "Group B" after Group A, "for Defendant" after Plaintiff), or a dual/plural anaphor collecting the named pair ("In both of them", "In both materials"). It stays near zero for first mentions with no counterpart, for repeated or unrelated substitute referents, and for two parties acting jointly or in agreement, whose mutuality vocabulary (mutual, agreement, relationship, cooperation) its negative output suppresses.

Fires on the word that expresses how often or at what rate an event happens, when it modifies an event that comes after it: indefinite-frequency adverbs placed before the verb ('Do your emotions sometimes/often/occasionally/frequently [rarely, usually, regularly weaker] dictate', strongest inside questions and weak in plain declaratives), the rate article or quantifier before a unit ('three times a year', 'twice a day', 'every 5 minutes', 'X percent of the time', 'spending more and more time'). It also fires on the closely related 'afraid/scared/reluctant to' (an inclination about whether the action will happen). It stays near zero for non-frequency adverbs (really, also, personally), for 'never' and 'always', for 'per'/'this' in place of the rate 'a', for sentence-initial 'Sometimes', and for frequency words after the verb ('go to the park often').

Retrospective detector of a discourse pivot: the pole fires on a contrast/update marker (but, however, sentence-initial Now/Next, or a but/how/what/why question) only when the preceding context establishes a success, expectation, concession, or completed background item and the peak introduces its limitation, exception, unresolved remainder, or next development. The same surface tokens without that two-part setup (plain 'and'-coordination, intra-clause 'but', adverbial 'right now', or a question asked without prior concession) stay quiet.

Fires on a segment token (usually starting with '.', '/', '-' or a version digit) two or more segments into a URL, namespace URI or dotted/slashed import path when the segments before it spell a familiar, often-copied boilerplate string, so the segment completes a memorized canonical path: schemas.android[.com], msdn.microsoft.com/en[-us], code.jquery.com[/jquery], github.com/Azure[/go], android.support.v[7], django[.db], org.apache.commons.net[.]. Replacing an earlier segment with an unfamiliar name (example, zorblat, x9) mostly removes it, generic URLs and file paths (www.google.com/search, C:\Users\..., com.example.myapp) and ordinary prose stay near zero, and memorized prose or message boilerplate ('error: no known class method', traceback 'line 10,') gives only weak to moderate activity.

Fires on the preposition or determiner that opens the interlocutor slot right after a word naming an act of interviewing, telling or reporting, questioning, surveying or recording: 'interview with', 'confirmed to', 'statement to', 'speaking to', 'told [the]', 'interviewed/questioned/photographed/surveyed by', 'phone call with', '(return) phone calls'. The peak is usually on 'with/to/by' (or 'the' / the outlet name just after it), whoever the interlocutor turns out to be, and activity is weak (<0.2 of max) when the same preposition follows a non-communicative head ('partnership with', 'returned to', 'funded by', 'walking to'). A weaker secondary activity (about 0.3-0.6 of max) appears on the digits of four-digit years that date a reported or studied event ('in 2004', 'June 2018').

This pole is a retrospective detector for the token that carries a time value in the text: the unit of an elapsed duration right after a quantity (minutes, min, mins, hours, h, seconds, strongest for sub-day units, reaching 1.8-2.2 of the 2.36 max), a clock or calendar instant (the ':' inside 17:48:35, the '–' of a date range such as August 17-20, 3:30 pm, 12 July 2021), and calendar or periodicity words used temporally (Saturday 1.08, Friday 0.89, July 0.70, weekend 0.69, weekly 0.66, duration 0.65, tonight 0.91 in a neutral carrier frame). It is not a general quantity, unit or token detector: the identical frame with a non-temporal unit (kilograms, metres, litres, volts, percent, mph, all 0.00-0.22) or with an ordinary noun (attempts 0.24, cats, people, shops) stays at the floor, 'minutes' in its record sense ('the minutes of the meeting', 0.27) stays at the floor, and the same nouns in an unrelated carrier are silent - with one admitted leftover I could not explain: a second family of computing identifiers (.Request, .Response, Command, requestType, .SelectCommand, query/SQL, execute) reaches 1.7-2.9 inside code-heavy text but only 0.0-0.6 in prose.

This pole is a retrospective detector for formal, specialized vocabulary: it fires on content words that carry technical, academic, institutional or code register - abstract quality nouns (validity, reliability, accuracy), technical terms and the long-word pieces they are built from (somatopsychic, polynucleotides, pulmonary embolism), and fixed specialized expressions (Special Session, namespace mpl, exports.down) - and it fires on more of a passage's content words when that passage is itself technical. It sits at the floor on simple everyday vocabulary in the same frame and position (dogs, tables, water, pleasant, road), on non-specialized counterparts of the same expressions (somatic, a general Session), and on ordinary narrative or dialogue prose.

The negative pole fires on the token that names a piece of geographic territory used as the location/scope of a phrase: either a region noun (area, region, province, state, city, county, district, borough, municipality) or a place name (England, Britain, Europe, Australia, Tanzania, California, San Francisco, the UK, the EC), typically as the object of a containment preposition (in, across, within, around) or as the head of 'the <place-name> area/region'. Its strength tracks how much of a set the territory delimits - quantified or generic phrases about things spread over the territory ('every hotel in the province', 'the museums in the city', 'buildings in the Ottawa area', 'endemic fauna of Tanzania', 'sportspeople from Presov') reach 0.4-1.9 on this neuron's 1.69 scale - and it falls to 0.00-0.20 for a definite-singular individual merely located in a country ('the hotel in England is expensive', 'the man in England was arrested'), for concrete object containers ('found in the office', 'in the drawer'), and when the place name is the clause subject ('England has many hotels') or a predicate-final adjunct ('Hotels are expensive in England').

The positive pole fires while the model is assembling or re-reading a distinctive multi-piece word - a proper name, acronym, camelCase/snake_case identifier, slash- or hyphen-joined compound, or scientific/technical term - peaking on one of the word's internal pieces (e.g. 'ar' in 'laparotomy', '.PRO'/'JECT' in 'PROJECT_ROOTS', 'gary' in '"Calgary') and dropping on the word's final piece. Its strength rises about 1.8x when the same item has already appeared earlier in the passage, is essentially zero on ordinary lowercase prose and on single-token function words, and its negative pole instead peaks on short common function words and boilerplate scaffolding (comment headers, 'Category:' labels, bylines).

Retrospectively fires on a qualifier that sits inside a phrase or relative clause restricting what a noun phrase picks out (or how far a claim holds): the negator of a reduced relative ('a service not listed', 'reactions not previously observed'), an epistemic or comparison adjective in a modifier ('variants of unknown significance', 'changes of unclear importance', 'with comparable/equivalent effects', 'with known effects'), a selective degree adverb ('particularly'/'especially', but not plain 'very'/'extremely'/'quite'), a partitive relative ('one of which'), and, in structured text, the value that fills a labelled slot ('Category:1903 births', a method's parameter list, an array-selector assignment). It is near zero on the same words used as a bare main-clause predicate ('the service is not listed', 'the changes have known effects', 'the subjects were particularly poor scorers') and on absolute magnitude or normality adjectives in the same slot ('beneficial', 'harmful', 'severe', 'major', 'typical', 'normal').

Fires on the content tokens of a hand-written literal data value in code, config, connection strings, paths or command lines: the sample or placeholder string a programmer typed in, such as a person's name, password, username, hostname, sheet or folder name, or the words demo/test. It is strongest on the first one or two subword tokens after the opening quote, '=', ':\\' or '-l' that begins the value, and on arbitrary or idiosyncratic values ("Maria", "demo", tecmint, students, C:\\BE). It is weak on conventional system or default values (Windows, Sheet1, Sales, localhost, 127.0.0.1) and near zero on keywords, variable references (null, None, $other, getpass()) and ordinary prose, even when the prose contains the same word.

This pole fires retrospectively on explicit scalar-quantity and measured-exchange constructions: equative frames (as much as), lower-bound thresholds (at least), tradeoff/exchange frames (at the expense of, sacrifice X for Y), sameness of amount, and precise measurements or dimensions with units. It peaks on the connective or measure token ('of', second 'as', 'for', 'least', digits) and stays quiet when the same function words appear in non-quantitative roles or when quantities are vague.

The negative pole fires on a token that designates a place or a position inside a structured space: most strongly on sub-national/administrative place nouns used locatively ('in a county', 'north-eastern Poland', 'the U.S. state of Illinois', 'in a village', 'several parts of the country') and on the locator/index tokens of a numbered address or lookup (the '[' and index of array accesses such as row[0], 'at index 5', 'page 42', 'chapter 7', 'Patent No. 11-325849', 'ZIP code 55089'). It is retrospective (truncating the text immediately after the peak leaves the peak unchanged, and ablating the pole at the peak leaves next-token probabilities unchanged) and is much weaker or silent on concrete object nouns in the same slot ('a house'), temporal references ('in 1998'), plain numerals in prose ('the total is 5') and place nouns in subject position ('The county is large' ~0.3 vs ~0.9 locatively); the same neuron's positive pole instead peaks on generic, vaguely enumerative prose ('a list of handy shortcuts for hosts, presenters, and attendees' = 1.2).

The pole fires retrospectively on the current token when it is a specific food or drink noun - cheese, wine, grapes, peaches, yoghurt, honey, jam, apples, oranges, eggs, fish, milk, rice, chocolate, cake, oil, sugar, lemon, lettuce, prunes, carrots, onions, tomatoes, cabbage, garlic, sausages - standing as a bare, undetermined item of an everyday eating, serving or recipe construction ('we ate bread and [[cheese]]' 0.99, 'the recipe calls for bread, [[cheese]], and wine' 1.11, 'we ate bread and [[grapes]]' 1.13, 'there was [[cheese]] on the table' 0.38), which is 0.4-1.3, i.e. 0.35-1.2 of the scan maximum. It stays at baseline when the same noun is determined or modified ('put the cheese on the table' 0.05, 'melt the cheese in a pan' -0.08, 'the cheese was fresh' 0.15, 'add the cheese and the wine to the pan' 0.10), when it is a generic staple rather than a specific item, even in the identical frame ('the recipe calls for butter' -0.03, 'we ate bread and butter' 0.16, and bread, meat, soup, salad, salt, pepper, flour, biscuits, lentils, steak all <= 0.20), and on ordinary narrative prose (<= 0.18).

This pole fires on tokens inside a run of symbolic mathematical notation: an expression in which digits, single-letter variables and arithmetic operators or exponents are combined without intervening words (e.g. '3x + 7 = 22', 'x^2 - 5x + 6 = 0', 'x^4/2 + x', '4a + 3b - 2a + 7b'), peaking on the operator, exponent or coefficient digit in the densest part of the expression, and growing stronger the more symbolic material precedes. It stays near zero in ordinary prose, and also in arithmetic or measurements written out in words ('three x plus seven equals twenty-two', 'twelve feet long', 'two cups of flour'), which is why the same content in words rather than symbols drops the activation.

The positive pole fires when the text refers to a specific-but-unnamed individual, or an indefinite subset, that is picked out of a plurality already live in the context, and it peaks on the determiner or quantifier that does the picking: partitives ('one of them', 'some of those', 'any one'), selection verbs taking a singular object ('select a partition' once the drive's partitions have been introduced, 'pick one', 'choose the second one'), and superlatives or ordinals that select one member ('the most serious', 'the first', 'which of the two'). It stays at the floor when the same word lacks that antecedent plurality ('You can just select a partition inside the drive.' alone: 0.21 vs 2.66 once a plural is introduced), when the phrase names a class rather than an instance ('it was one of the most serious': 0.14 vs 0.76 for 'the most serious happened'), and when the whole set is quantified or exactly counted ('all/each/both of them', 'two of them', 'three bicycles'), which drives the negative pole together with bare cardinal counts ('12 countries', 'eight rabbits').

This pole is a retrospective detector for text that is written in a fixed documentary format rather than free prose: it peaks on the token that fills a conventional slot of that format - a licence or copyright restriction clause ('without the express written permission of the publisher', 'the specific language governing permissions and limitations'), a patent preamble ('the [present] invention relates generally/broadly to'), a biographical parenthetical ('(born 28 July 1992)', '(b. 1992)'), a bibliographic citation line ('et al.'), a legal case caption ('..., a Corporation Not For Profit'), a URL path ('/post/2010/09/'), or a code import/annotation/HTML class name. It is the slot and not the token - 'permissions' to 'rights', 'generally' to 'broadly' and 'born' to 'b' all keep the peak where it is, while the identical clause in a plain sentence, in ordinary legal prose, or behind a narrative lead-in stays at or below 0.35, well under the 0.48 active threshold on the 1.91 scale; known leftovers are the rare political adverb 'legislatively', which fires on its own (judicially/statutorily/ministerially do not), and the code-notation family, which only reaches threshold inside a real code block.

The pole fires retrospectively on an approximator that supplies the value of an explicitly named measurement: 'about', 'around', 'roughly', 'approximately', 'nearly' or 'almost' directly before an amount, and 'or so' directly after one, when the clause names the measured attribute either as its subject ('the price/weight/distance/duration/delay/temperature/rate/probability/population/age/height/area/volume/speed is about ten ...') or as a measure verb ('costs', 'weighs', 'takes', 'lasts', 'measures', 'holds', 'covers', 'contains', 'reaches', 'earns', 'spends', 'paid', 'is worth' + about ten ...); the peak is on the approximator itself and is unaffected by the words that follow it. It stays near zero on the same words used in other roles -- topical 'about' and spatial 'around' ('talked about', 'walked around', 'The book is about ten dollars'), attributive measure phrases built on an adjective ('about thirty years old', 'about six feet tall', 'about ten metres long'), precise or boundary quantifiers inside the same measure frame ('exactly', 'precisely', 'at least', 'under', 'or more'), bare numbers, quantifiers of countable objects ('many people', 'several reasons', 'a couple of friends'), and plain intensifiers or frequency adverbs ('very', 'often', 'usually', 'generally', 'probably', 'relatively', 'particularly').

The negative pole is the non-human side of a person-referent feature: it fires retrospectively on a token that carries no human reference, and its peak in a snippet is the most strongly non-human content word there - a concrete object, substance, plant, animal or natural phenomenon ('pan', 'clouds', 'rain', 'nature', 'rates', 'mould', 'water'), or, when the snippet has none, a numeral or punctuation mark ('=', '0', '1', sentence-final '.'). It sits at the floor, with the positive pole firing instead, when the current token names a person or a group of people - above all kinship, social-role and collective nouns ('family', 'friend', 'colleague', 'neighbour', 'teacher', 'patient', 'child', 'children', 'students') - so a snippet whose content words are all person nouns is predicted inactive (measured: 'for the family' +1.9, 'the neighbour' +1.4, 'the friend' +1.5, 'the teacher' +0.8, 'the patient' +0.7, versus 'the table' +0.0 and 'the river' +0.0), while swapping a non-human subject or object for a person in an otherwise identical frame lowers the pole (in an otherwise identical frame, 'The workshop repaired...' peaks at 0.34 and 'Her brother repaired...' at 0.11, against a scan scale of 1.19).

L11/N4169- fires at the word that completes an ending or leave-taking expression, not on the topic of endings: the preposition or particle directly after a departure or close-of-period verb ('left/leaves/departed/quit' + with, without, behind, after, in; 'ended/closed' + with, without), the leave-taking word 'goodbye', and 'last'/'final' inside a definite or possessive noun phrase that names the final instance of something ('his last game', 'the last of the firewood', 'for the last time', 'in his last moments'), together with the head noun that such a phrase modifies ('their last game', 'final moments'). It stays near zero in the identically shaped beginnings and continuations ('first', 'initial', 'next', 'latest', 'began/started with', 'stayed with', 'left the building at eleven'), for 'last' meaning most-recent ('last week's meeting', 'the previous summer') and for bare ending vocabulary ('finished with a win', 'over', 'until', 'the final report'), so the trigger is the closing construction rather than the token or the concept alone.

Fires on the connective that hands a just-named plural category noun over to a list of its members: most reliably ', including' after a plural noun naming a class of entities (countries, cities, species, universities, artists, dishes; 0.4-1.0 of max, above threshold in >90% of 'several <class>, including' cases with ~500 tokens of prior text), and less reliably ', such as' / ', like' / ', notably' in the same slot (0.3-0.8, stronger in long documents, weak when there is no comma before them). It stays below 25% of max on 'including' that adds a component to an amount, price or duration ('the invoice/rent/fee, including tax', 'ten euros, including a drink', 'four hours, including stops', 'All costs, including tax'), after generic artifact categories (tools, instruments, materials), and on 'for example', 'for instance' and usually ', e.g.'; known leftovers predicted active are '<nationality adjective> state/province/canton of <Name>' ('the German state of Bavaria', not 'the state of Bavaria' or 'the city of Paris'), the WordPress footer 'This entry was posted ... and is filed under <Tag>', a clause-final ':' that opens an elaboration ('single-handedly: with ...', 'visible at once: the ...'; not reported speech 'He answered: ...'), LaTeX/code operators (' +', ' =', '\frac'), and a diffuse background (~0.6% of ordinary tokens reach 0.29-0.5) that makes most texts longer than ~150 tokens active, so only short texts without these triggers are predicted inactive.

This pole fires at a continuation boundary (a comma, 'and'/'or', sentence period, opening paren, or word-internal joint) when it extends an already-established, highly predictable formulaic run: a repeated list of same-domain co-occurring items (foods, colors, compass points, numbers), a scalar 'X or more/not Y' frame, an acronym expansion of a long technical noun phrase, or the inside of a long compound/identifier, with strength ramping on second-or-later boundaries.
