The same punctuation opening a run, or joining a novel unpredictable juxtaposition after a short simple phrase (e.g. commas in 'rent, utilities, fees, taxes' or '(' after 'The magnetic resonance imaging'), does not fire.

Fires on the first token that continues a sentence (mostly ',' but also ' (', ' -', ' and', ' however') right after a short, terse main clause that ends on a bare predicate whose complement is left implicit and recoverable from earlier context: VP ellipsis ('It did,', 'Martin doesn't,', 'You can,'), a bare adjective or intransitive verb ('It is possible,', 'They are still looking,', 'it was rarer,'), or a stranded preposition ('a model of,'). It is strongest when the clause is a curt answer to or comment on a topic set up well before (e.g. 'It is possible,' answering a 'Can I...?' question), weak when the clause carries an explicit object or complement ('You can subclass FileInputFormat,'), and near-silent on semicolons, on commas after introductory adverbials ('Yes,', 'In the winter,') and on list commas; leftovers include decimal and thousands separators after a number that could have ended the clause ('$9[.]38', '300[,]000').

This pole fires on the token that continues or completes the currently open clause or phrase: the grammatically expected next piece such as a noun completing a possessive or attributive phrase, a relativizer after its head noun, a verb or copula completing the predicate, an infinitive 'to' after its trigger, or a comma resuming the main clause after a fronted adjunct. It stays quieter at sentence onsets, after sentence-final breaks, or when the expected continuation is replaced by a token that cannot fill the slot.

The negative pole fires on the connector or degree word that carries a specification -- a preposition or definite article (' of', ' on', ' to', ' in', ' the'), a relative/complementizer pronoun, a degree or quantity word (' least', ' exactly', ' one'), or the head word that opens such a specification (' contain', ' stored', ' silent') -- when the clause read so far states the contents, attributes, requirements or status of a definite concrete entity (a password rule, a recipe's ingredients, a legal charge, a place's inventory, a formal fact). It stays at baseline for the same tokens in personal, imperative or ad-hoc sentences ('You need at least two hours', 'She has at least three cats', 'He depends on his parents') and in plain narration ('The cat sat on the mat': ' on' 0.09 there against 0.28 in 'landed on the Moon').

This pole fires where a document reproduces or identifies a string instead of composing new prose: at the onset of a direct quotation (the opening quote mark " " / " “ " / " ' " / " ‘ ", or a mis-typed " ” ", and the first one or two words inside it, strongest when that first word is a dialogue opener such as Yes, Yeah, No, Oh, Sure or Hello) regardless of which verb or phrase introduces it (said, replied, declared, whispered, 'saying things like', 'phrases such as', 'the word', 'the phrase', 'the message', 'Best Line:', or a colon), and on the all-caps licence/file constants LICENSE, COPYING and COPYRIGHT (strongly) and AUTHORS, CONTRIBUTORS and NOTICE (more weakly) when the text points the reader at that file, plus the same identifying job for people in reference frames (the abbreviation period of a personal initial like 'W.C.' or 'Rosemary C.', and a personal name in the predicate of a kinship list like 'His parents were William (d.1784) and Agnes'). It stays below the active threshold on ordinary narrative and descriptive prose, on the same utterance reported without quotation marks ('said that the car was here', 'said hello'), on other file names and lower-case spellings (README, MIT, GPL, manual, documentation, 'license'), on ordinary proper nouns in plain sentences ('Prince William visited the school', 'The team included John Smith, Mary Jones and Peter Brown', 'The cities were Boston and Chicago'), on a bare year inside a prose sentence, and on a quotation that starts a text with no preceding narration; its strength is graded with the lead-in, needing roughly an attributive clause (raw strength 0.63 for 'Maria looked at the mayor and said "hello"', versus 0.27 for the five-word 'He said "hello".', against an active threshold near 0.33).

The negative pole is a retrospective detector of the typographic line boundary of an informational article: it peaks on the newline token that closes a standalone label line - a heading, sub-headline, caption, pull-quote, case-citation line, date header or one-word section label ('Background', 'Personal history', 'Alternatives') - and, as a graded secondary family, on the temporal adjunct that anchors a paragraph or clause ('On Thursday,', 'That afternoon,', 'on Saturday'), the spike landing on the day name or adverb and its closing comma. It stays at the floor for those same heading words folded into a running sentence, for paragraph breaks between ordinary sentences, for the same temporal words in a parenthetical aside or used non-temporally ('2007 people'), and in fiction, dialogue, instructional and persuasive text; amplitude is graded by how much the surrounding document reads like a scraped article, so clean synthetic expository prose reproduces only part of the heading response (a leftover this class acknowledges).

The negative pole fires on the token that closes an insertion spliced into a running structure: the ')' (or '!)', '])', '),') that ends a parenthetical aside, the second '—'/'--' of a dash-bracketed aside, or the newline that ends an in-line comment spliced into a line of code — i.e. exactly the point where the interrupted clause, sentence or code line resumes (the resumption word right after the closer often carries a smaller echo of the same activation). It stays at the floor when the same words are written flat, for comma-delimited asides (4 to 10 times weaker), for parentheses that belong to the clause itself such as notation ('f(x)', 'sin(x)') or labels ('Fig. 4', 'Table 2'), and for code lines with no comment, while inside a real aside the amplitude is graded — largest when the inserted material carries a qualifying fact or number, smallest for a bare single-word label or adverb.

The pole fires on the linking function word of a specific, name- or term-like nominal: overwhelmingly ' of' (and the ' the' that immediately follows it), plus ' per', ' in', ' by', ' below', ' than', ' about' in dates, rates and measured quantities, and digits/operators inside numbers and formulas, at the point where the left context has already built a definite noun phrase denoting a particular institution, document, body part, rule or quantity ('the local chapter of', 'the Wisconsin chapter of', 'the Civil Rights Act of', 'the long head of', 'the law of', 'the 22nd day of', 'the History of the County of'). It stays at zero, and its negative pole instead fires, when the same preposition only joins a bare generic or quantitative head to its complement ('the number of', 'the importance of', 'the use of', 'the first chapter of the book', 'The Battle of Hastings') or sits in a heading ('Overview of', 'Table of Contents'); the peak sits on the function word and collapses on the following content word, so the reading is retrospective, fixed by the left context and insensitive to which designation actually follows.

Fires on the opening tokens of a conjunct that follows a bare comma (or a line break) with no conjunction, i.e. the second or later member of an asyndetic list or parallel series ("dimers, trim[ers]", "word processor, office [suite]", "easier to read, [more]", "six physicians, [six]", "1. ..., [2].", comma-spliced parallel clauses "shape, responses [were]"). It peaks on the token that completes the new conjunct's head (often the second token after the comma). It stays near zero when the conjunct is introduced by 'and'/'or', a semicolon or a full stop, and after non-coordinating commas (introductory adverbials, subordinate clauses, appositives, vocatives); single-token items in plain noun lists fire only weakly.

The positive side of this neuron is the counterpart of its verified negative pole: it fires on a token that is a later/internal piece of a machine-formatted string - a snake_case/camelCase identifier or argument, a dotted qualified import name, a number such as a year or version, or a repeated format element - when that string sits inside a code, markup, comment or template construct with a fixed, rehearsed form (e.g. `_length` in `CharField(max_length = 255)`, `files` in `{% load staticfiles %}`, `.slf` in `import org.slf4j.LoggerFactory;`, the interior digits of `2016` in a `// Copyright` header, the third `M` of `"EEEE d MMMM y"`, `-` in `encoding="utf-8"`). It stays near zero when the same words occur in prose, on whole-word tokens, on pieces of ordinary alphabetic words, and on the rare names that drive the negative pole (Coldwell Banker, Daler-Rowney, HMC5883L), which is the distinction the two poles draw: rare name whose completion must be retrieved (negative) versus familiar machine-formatted string whose continuation is set by the format (positive).

Fires on the interior pieces (second through second-to-last) of a rare, recognisable string that the tokenizer splits into several subword, letter or digit pieces: brand and place names (Coldwell| Bank|er, Daler|-R|owney, Ilfrac|om|be, Eyjafjallajokull), Latin set phrases (res ipsa lo|quit|ur, incertae| sed|is), code identifiers (execute_from|_command|_line, frozen|_string|_literal, s|.r|.o) and model or error codes (HMC58|8|3L, V6|1|7F, C20|6|1, ed255|1|9). It peaks once the earlier pieces have identified the string and more pieces must follow. It stays near zero on the first piece, on the final completing piece, on common words and phrases, on unfamiliar gibberish (Qorvexlandipur), and when an earlier piece is changed so the string is no longer recognisable (Coldwater Banker, Dalek-Rowney, 'error at2061').

Fires at the seam where an element of an already-established repeated text format ends and the next slot of that format begins — the import slot after a Java package header, later entries of a JSON/INI/SQL/email-header/comment/diff/citation/table/numbered-list block — and, in prose, at the quote-close+attribution or the comma/dash that closes a long parenthetical insertion whose embedded clause has a lexical verb and its complement. The trigger is the structural boundary rather than the surface token: the same `import`, `,"`, comma or newline in free prose, as a lone or first occurrence, or after a short or verbless/copular quotation stays below threshold.

Retrospective detector of metatextual reference: the pole fires across a span that points at the text being written or read, at another written text, or at a named part of one - 'in this article / post / blog / chapter / section / page / report / guide / piece', 'This article will...', 'discussed in Chapter 7', 'see / refer to Section 3, Appendix A, page 12', 'for more information, see X', 'click here', 'if you are reading this'. It is not a publication-noun or see/read/click token detector: generic, indefinite or physical uses of the same nouns ('an article about fishing', 'articles of clothing', 'the newspaper article was published yesterday') and the same verbs with a non-document object outside the pointer frame ('see the doctor', 'click the button') stay near zero, while the formulaic pointer frame still fires when its object is a person ('for more information, see the doctor'); the pole's write direction promotes no specific next token (Jacobian kurtosis 3.3) and suppresses the publication vocabulary it has just read ( blog, Blog, Newsletter, Tutorial, ISBN, ISSN, 出版社, 博文).

Fires retrospectively on a token that is a conventional, lexically fitting continuation completing the immediately preceding multi-token frame (a copula after a conjoined plural subject, 'of' after a complement-taking noun, a particle after its verb, a characteristic predicate after its subject, or a speech verb closing quoted dialogue); the same syntactic slot with an unfitting word, or the same function token without its licensing frame, stays low.

The negative pole of L13/N439 fires when the text sets a second, alternative referent against the one already in focus: it peaks on contrastive/substitutive phrases ('in favour of', 'instead of', 'in place of', 'rather than', 'as opposed to', 'compared to/with', 'in contrast to', 'unlike') and on the later members of an enumeration or alternative list ('X, Y and Z', 'X or Y', especially after 'like/such as/including'), the strength scaling with how explicitly the alternative is marked. It stays near the floor for proposition-level negation ('not', 'never'), for clause-linking contrast ('but', 'although', 'however', 'whereas', 'while'), for 'and' that merely sequences two clauses, and for 'between X and Y'; it is retrospective (zero-ablating the pole on its top examples leaves next-token probabilities essentially unchanged, KL 2e-5).

The negative pole fires on the tokens that close a statement or expression in code and mathematical notation: the `false`/`true`/`None` literal that ends a `return` or a boolean assignment (or the bare `return`/`break`/`continue` keyword that ends its own statement), the `;` and `}` that terminate the statement and its `if`/`while`/`for` block, and the binary operator (`-`, `=`, `==`, `) -`) that follows a completed operand in an equation. The pattern is surface-level (a code-like line fires even inside a comment or string), and ordinary prose and code without such a closing construct stay quiet.

The negative pole fires on a personal pronoun (you, I, we, she, he, they; weaker for me/your/her and for 'one'/'someone') that opens the subject slot of a new, usually subordinate or embedded clause right after a linking word (when, if, in case, should, so, hoping, help, let, sparing, what), whose referent is NOT an earlier-mentioned person: deictic or generic 'you/I/we', or a hypothetical 'she/he/they' in text about objects or advice. It is the contrast to the positive pole (pronouns that refer back): it drops sharply when a third-person pronoun has a matching earlier human antecedent ('The nurse ... when she'), and stays near zero on 'it', on names and full noun phrases in the same slot, on sentence-initial main-clause pronouns, and on non-pronoun words, while deictic 'you' is unaffected by an earlier person.

The negative pole of Qwen2.5-0.5B L13/N1963 fires on the punctuation token that opens a parenthetical/aside interpolation inside a running sentence: strongest on an em dash or spaced double hyphen (scan means 0.45-0.53, peaks 1.6-1.9), weaker on an en dash, and weakly but reliably on an opening parenthesis (mean 0.19 across the scan's 804 ' (' tokens versus 0.03 for an arbitrary token; usually below the 0.25 x max active threshold, but up to 1.2 when the parenthesis holds a heavy apposition or citation). It is retrospective - it peaks on the delimiter itself, with no rise at the preceding token (0.02-0.03) and only 0.02-0.04 on the next token - and is silent on the matching closing dash or bracket (all 403 scanned ')' tokens and the second dash of a dash-opened aside score ~0), on commas, colons and semicolons, on dashes at the start of a list line, and on en dashes inside numeric ranges; its Jacobian-lens write promotes opening-paren tokens (' (', ' ("', ' ([', ' (<'), the canonical spelling of that same 'parenthesis open' state.

The negative pole of L13/N2052 is a Wikipedia category-markup detector: it fires when the text contains a wiki category declaration ('Category:<term>', and even more strongly '[[Category:<term>]]'), ramping through 'Category' and ':' to a peak on the opening tokens of the category term, and it fires hardest when that term begins with a 4-digit year ('Category:1903 births/films', peak ~2.0 locally and 3.4 in full articles), less for word terms ('Category:Italian cyclists' ~1.4) and single words ('Category:Physics' ~0.9). The trigger is the wiki category syntax plus a year-like value, not the tokens or the year itself: running prose ('He was born in 1903', 0.2), ordinary label lines ('Name: John Smith' 0.07, 'Year: 1903 births' 0.46), CSV rows and infobox fields stay near zero, and a minority of strong activations (5 of the 20 scan examples, in non-wiki prose) are not explained by this hypothesis.

The positive pole fires on the classifying, domain-specifying vocabulary of written expository prose - the word that states what kind of thing, or in what field or respect, the text is talking about: relational adjectives and noun classifiers such as medical, clinical, surgical, hospital, patient, official, academic, scientific, industrial, biological, brain, molecular, viral, prior (art), in vivo, state-of-the-art, and domain adverbs of respect such as internally or technically. It is near zero on qualitative adjectives (old, heavy, happy), generic determiners and pronouns, and on conversational, narrative, lyric or list-like text, and the same classifying word fires roughly twice as strongly when the surrounding passage is technical/expository than when it is casual.

The negative pole detects a reference to a historical period - a year, decade or century expression - and fires while that period is being read: it climbs from the leading '1' and peaks on the second or third digit once the century is fixed ('19' in 19th/1900s/1950s/1990s is the strongest form, 3.6-4.5 against the audit's 4.17 maximum, with 18xx ~2.2-2.9 and 1600s/1700s/20xx ~1.3-1.9 in the same frame, and all 19xx decades are indistinguishable), stays high on the trailing 'th'/'s'/'century', and fires moderately (1.0-1.5) on era-defining terms of the modern past (Soviet, World War II, Cold War, Victorian era); on this audit's 200k-token scan 1.8% of tokens lie inside a date/period expression, yet they hold 98% of the tokens above 2.0 (mean strength 0.51 there versus 0.03 elsewhere). It stays near zero when the same digits are quantities, codes, ordinals or addresses ('1876 dollars' 0.50, '1876 units' 0.12, '19th street' 0.12, 'Her phone number was 1876' 0.02), on antiquity (Roman 0.25, pharaoh 0.19, 'ancient' 0.09), on vague past talk ('in the past' 0.31) and on present-day prose; its transported output direction (TV/television/Sony/broadcast promoted, ancient/Romans/parchment suppressed) is diffuse with next-token KL about 8e-4, so the mechanism is retrospective and the weak positive pole (max 2.32 on the same scan) does not carry this feature.

The positive pole fires on the token that carries a new instance of an already-established parallel series: the second and later members of a coordinate list (England, [[Wales]], Northern Ireland; Google, [[Yahoo]], MSN; flour, [[eggs]], [[sugar]], butter; Paris, [[Berlin]], Rome; He is tall, [[dark]], and handsome) and the varying part of a repeated template (boxHeight/[[boxLength]]/boxWidth, dbUser/[[dbPass]]/dbSchema, pepB-/[[pepN]]-/pepA-, font-oti/[[font-otl]]/font-oto, the repeated digit pair of #434343, the continuation marker \cdots in $k_1,\cdots,k_n$, repeated CSS/table rows), rising from the floor on the first member (0.00 for England, Google, apples, Paris, red) to 0.6-1.5 on interior members. It stays at the floor for those same words outside a series (Wales 0.00, Yahoo 0.00, Windows 0.00, bananas 0.00), for non-enumerative commas (However, ...; In 2019, ...; appositive commas) and for attributive adjective stacks inside a noun phrase (a big, red, shiny hat), and it falls back toward the floor on a short list's final item after a closing 'and'/'or' (bananas 0.08, blue 0.00, timelines 0.00, butter 0.07).

The positive pole fires on the word that states a share of a whole in expository prose - fraction and share nouns ('a third', 'a quarter', 'a fifth', 'half', 'three quarters', 'per cent'/'cent', '%', 'the majority', 'one in five') and the 'the size of X' magnitude comparison - peaking there at 0.5-1.3 of its 1.25 scan maximum, with the rest of the quantity phrase around a count or a per-cent expression (magnitude words, counting numerals and their units) elevated less strongly at 0.1-0.5. It is near zero (<=0.2) on the same words used non-quantitatively ('cut it in half', 'a quarter in the parking meter', 'a third kind', 'third-party'), on dates, prices and page numbers, and in narrative prose, while the same share word still moves three- to tenfold with the clause it sits in ('a fifth of the members had left' ~0.0 alone, ~1.3 after 'The study found that', ~1.0 after 'The survey showed that', ~0.3 after 'the neighbours knew that'); this is the same unit whose negative pole is the program-identifier detector in source code, and the two poles are complementary - a code snippet drives it to -1.6 with a positive reading of 0.15, a proportion statement to +1.3 with a negative reading of -0.06.

The negative pole fires on the word-pieces of program identifiers (class, type, function, variable and package names) inside source code, peaking on the identifier's leading piece - ' Weather' in WeatherTodayModel, ' V'/'pn'/'Sites' in VpnSitesClient, ' aut' in autorest, ' graphics' in 'var graphics' - and staying elevated across the rest of the name, equally for declared and referenced names. It is near zero on language keywords, punctuation, operators, numbers and string text, and falls to roughly a tenth of peak when the very same words appear in ordinary prose (a code comment is intermediate); strength does vary between names (' Module', 'Sites', 'Sampling', 'Multi' fire several times harder than 'Client', 'Model', 'Foo'), which is the residual token-identity confound.

Fires retrospectively when the current token continues an already-established repeated formatting template, i.e. the third-or-later same-format item such as successive quoted utterances, forum comments, markdown headings, JSON key lines, dated diary entries, filmography/config entries or code methods, with strength growing as more same-format items accumulate; stays weak on an isolated first heading, entry or quote and on ordinary prose paragraph or sentence breaks with no repeating template.

The pole marks the close of a free-standing direct quotation: it peaks on the punctuation token that ends a quotation which occupies its own sentence - typically the comma-glued close ',”', ',"', '!”' or '?”' that hands the utterance back to the narrator, as in '“We need cash,” he said' - and it is near zero on the identical close-quote token when the quotation is embedded in the running sentence (after a reporting verb, 'He said “We need cash,” and left'; as a quoted term, 'The phrase “we need cash,” was used'; or after a mid-sentence colon), on scare quotes closing mid-phrase, on '”' used for inches, on opening quotes, and on a quotation that ends its sentence with '.”' at a paragraph break. Within the free-standing class the strength is graded rather than categorical: it grows with the amount of preceding news-style reporting (about 1.2 with no context, 2.8 after one reportative paragraph, 3.9 after two, up to 5.9 in long articles), is suppressed to near zero when another quotation close falls within a few tokens, and does not depend on what follows the close (the same token fires whether an attribution, a conjunction or another clause comes next).

Retrospective chunk-completion detector: the pole peaks on the word that completes a conventional local chunk opened by the preceding token(s) -- canonically a sentence- or phrase-initial common noun after a determiner/article (The/A orchestra, recipe, senator, museum), and as offshoots the expected token after a code keyword (numpy to as, FROM to users), a verb licensing a preposition (hiked to to), a comma licensing 'and', a digit continuing a number, or the second half of a fixed collocation (central to bank, golden to brown). The same word without its conventional opener (as after 'served', orchestra after 'His', senator mid-sentence) or an unfamiliar word in the same slot (mat to xyz, brown to xyz) activates weakly or not at all, while changes after the peak leave the peak unchanged.

This pole fires where a document's or record's metadata block - a run of short label-plus-value fragments such as a title, byline, date, price, score, or attribute fields like 'Price: 12', 'Weight: 3 kg', 'Material: cotton' - closes and running body prose begins. It peaks on the block's closing token (a newline, period or bracketed title end) and on the body's first word, its strength grows with the number of fields already read (one bare label is usually sub-threshold, three or more attribute fields are strong), and it stays quiet when the same facts are written as sentences, at a paragraph break between two prose sentences, after a bare value-less heading such as 'Note' or 'Chapter One', and after dialogue speaker labels.

N4610- is a retrospective detector for the read-out of a low-frequency, domain-specific word: it fires on the token at which a rare content word becomes identified - usually the second BPE piece of a multi-token rare word (K|iv|u, Stone|h|enge, Hir|anyak|ashyapu, super|abs|orbent, Mach|-Z|ehnder, cata|le|psy, io.gitlab.art|urb|osch) and otherwise the distinctive word inside a specialised fixed phrase (coronal 'mass' ejections, institutional 'review' board, burden 'of' proof, ineffective assistance 'of' counsel). It scales with word rarity and with how established the word already is - a rare word's first mention is weak (0.0-0.3) while a re-mention or a strongly predicting frame raises it to 0.6-2.3 - whereas ordinary common words, common multi-piece words (somebody, nevertheless, understand), common phrases (peer review, cup of tea, state of the art), word-initial function words and never-seen nonsense strings (Blubberhouse, Xylophonia) stay near zero.

The negative pole fires on the token that is a word-internal fragment of an unfamiliar proper name: the interior or final subword piece of a rare surname, place name or coined/foreign-looking name that the model has no familiar lexical item or known entity for (Lovell 'ell' 2.4 of max 3.8, Standish 'ish' 2.2, Jodrell 'rell' 2.2, Amundsen 'sen' 3.2, Plesetsk 'etsk' 1.6, Menzies 'ies' 1.6, Schulich 'ich' 1.9, coined 'Zarvoski' 'ki' 2.3), with activation growing along the name so that the first piece stays near zero (' Lov' 0.25, ' Menz' 0.09, ' Zar' 0.41) and the last piece is strongest; on the held-out scan windows this is the only thing that reaches the 0.25x-max (about 0.94) active threshold in 5% of 32-token windows. It stays below that threshold on the identical fragments when the word is familiar English even if multi-piece and capitalized (internationalization 'ization' 0.0, multidisciplinary 0.09, Polytechnic 0.6, Pleistocene 0.6, telescope 0.02), when the earlier piece of the name is missing from the prompt ('elson-MIT' 0.3 vs 'Lemelson-MIT' 3.5, 'Menz ies' 0.35, bare 'ies' 0.02), and for names the model already holds as known entities or single familiar tokens (Churchill 1.4, Manchester 0.9, Shakespeare 0.65, 'Roald Amundsen' 0.5 against bare 'Amundsen' 3.2); the only non-name tokens seen at threshold are single commas or digits inside dense citation lists, at about 1.0.

The pole fires on tokens that carry the surface syntax of machine-formatted or templated text rather than authored prose: HTML/XML tag names and angle-bracket delimiters, the quotes, keys and delimiters of serialized records (JSON, YAML, CSV, INI), machine timestamp and record lines such as 'Mon, 08 Jun 2017 10:00:00 GMT', entity codes and URL fragments, and the fixed words of chat templates, licence headers and other boilerplate formulas. The same words inside an ordinary sentence - a date spelled out in prose, a 'the', 'if', 'system' or 'div' in running text, a comma inside a sentence - leave it inactive.

This pole is a sparse retrospective detector (near-zero bulk over ~200k tokens, max 1.84) that fires on the function-word or evaluative-word joints of clauses stating a precaution, requirement, maintenance condition, or damage/malfunction contingency (e.g. 'avoids any nasty accidents with', 'be careful when handling', 'must contain', 'are dropped ... may'); the same surface tokens stay near zero in neutral reporting, bare punctual imperatives, direct harm statements without precautionary framing, and at sentence or piece onsets. Single sentences give weak-to-moderate activation; the top tail needs a longer cautionary passage. Acknowledged leftovers: neutral project-credit ('initial direction') and spec-conditional ('may be parsed') peaks are not covered.

Fires at the onset of a numeral that states a cardinal quantity (a count or amount of things: subjects, people, hours, fans, donations, dollars, points, votes), peaking on the space token, '$', 'n =' or first digit just before the digits, and strongest when the frame sets up a sizable quantity ('a combined total of', 'over', 'about', 'more than $', '(n =', 'needs', 'population of'). It stays near zero when the same digits are an identifier or date (years, 'in 1960', page/room/ward/form numbers, 'Fig.', postal codes, coordinates) and when no number follows, so it encodes 'a quantity count is starting here', not digit tokens per se.

Fires on tokens inside spans that continue character-for-character, i.e. verbatim memorized strings: OSS license-header sentences ('This Source Code Form is subject to the terms of the ... License', the AS-IS disclaimer), court-caption formulas ('PER CURIAM' under 'UNITED STATES COURT OF APPEALS', '... CIRCUIT'), tool-output and template spans (netstat rows, docker info lines, '(ABSTRACT TRUNCATED AT 250 WORDS)', docfx/javadoc markup like '<!--[if IE]><![endif]-->'), box-drawn comment headers, Windows GAC strong-name paths (v4.0_4.0.0.0__b03f5f7f11d50a3a), and other fixed runs such as hex digits, aligned whitespace columns and rare word fragments (' abs|ou|lt|ely'); activation rises along such a span and peaks where the upcoming token is most certain (measured Spearman +0.63 between pole strength and next-token certainty, -0.63 with next-token surprise), which is why the very same fragments (' subject', 'f', ' C', 'RED') are inert in ordinary prose. Retrospective: the fixed span is already on the page, and the pole's output promotes its literal continuation (identifier/path/format fragments like 'f', '0', '_MS', ' terms', ' tcp', whitespace runs) while suppressing generic word continuations (' to', ' and', ' a', ','); ablation moves probability off exactly those continuation tokens.

Fires on text about cultivating crops or plants (agronomy/horticulture: fields, soil, fertilizer or pesticide application, irrigation, weeds competing with crops, plants grown under given conditions, harvests, drought, lawns): activation switches on at the first crop/plant-cultivation word and stays high over the following tokens of that clause, usually peaking on the verbs, prepositions, conjunctions and punctuation after the topic word (e.g. 'applied', 'for', 'under', 'during', 'and', '.') rather than on the topic noun itself; one short sentence is enough, no long context is required. It is weak (under about 30% of max) for livestock/animal husbandry and forestry/logging, and near zero for the same sentence frames about non-agricultural subjects (finance, plumbing, cell culture, computers, cooking, code).

This pole fires on the reference apparatus of formal, templated text rather than on what that text says: metadata field labels and their colons in a paper header ('author:', 'address:', 'bibliography:'), citation and numbered cross-reference markers ('[12, 13]', '([@bib26]', 'section 4', 'problem 6', 'Aim 3', '10.1002/mrm.27594'), section headings with their underline rules, and formulaic openers such as 'To identify ... we studied' or 'The purpose of this study was to'. Running narrative prose, plain bullet lists, config YAML, JSON and code stay far below it (peak under 0.2 of max), and the peak at a metadata label rises with how much front matter has already been read (deleting the abstract or the address fields drops 'author:' from 2.58 to 2.04 and 2.26).

This negative pole fires on a clause that restates content already present in the same context: it peaks on the answer, heading-repeat, definition or summary that re-uses the distinctive content words of an earlier question, heading or claim (the FAQ/definition pattern), and its strength grows with the number of echoed content words (none shared ~0.1-0.3 of the 1.386 max, three or four shared ~0.9-1.3), saturating around three. It falls back to baseline when the clause introduces new vocabulary even on the same topic, and its output direction barely moves the next-token distribution (Jacobian kurtosis 3.4, lens agreement 0%, measure_lookahead KL 7e-5), so it is retrospective rather than predictive.

Fires on website cookie/tracking-consent notice boilerplate, i.e. a site telling its visitor that it uses cookies (or analytics/tracking) to give them the best experience and that continuing to browse/use the site means they agree (English, French and other languages). Activity builds across the notice clause and peaks on the sentence-ending punctuation (or the following 'By'/'This') right after a 'we use cookies to ... experience/website' or 'this site uses cookies' clause; it is near zero when cookies are a topic rather than a notice (browser cookie how-tos, studies about cookie banners) or food (bake/eat cookies, jar of cookies), and weak (~0.15-0.45 of max) on adjacent legal boilerplate like reCAPTCHA notices, newsletter sign-up privacy lines and GPL licence headers.

This pole fires on generic continuation tokens (articles, pronouns, conjunctions, prepositions, light adverbs, or routine nouns like 'sample'/'police') when the preceding long-range context describes an institutional procedure that inspects, tests, adjudicates, monitors, or records a person or item — arrest, drug test, trial, audit, detention, medical check, school assessment, or data collection. The same sentence frames describing casual, social, or benign events with no such procedure stay near zero, while the procedure alone (even with a benign verdict) keeps it partly active.

The pole fires while the model spells out the identity of a software artifact: it is active across a dotted software version number in a software/computing context (the digits and periods of 'django 1.2.3', 'Ubuntu 20.04', 'v2.4.1', 'firmware 15.2', peaking at or just before the first separator after the major number), and more weakly on the tokens of software product/framework/OS names themselves (' django', ' nginx', 'oa' in Modoboa, 'jango' in Django). The computing context can be a software name anywhere in the recent text ('I use django. The fix landed in 1.2.3' fires on the version) or plain engineering register ('the bug was fixed in 1.2.3' fires; 'the car was fixed in 1.2.3' does not), while the same surface forms outside software stay near zero: decimals in ordinary prose ('1.2.3 cups', '3.5 percent', '1.5 mg'), sentence-final periods, and hardware model numbers or proper nouns (Toyota Corolla 2014, iPhone 12, Xeon E5-2690, Mary in London).

N366+ is a retrospective code line-terminator detector: it fires on the whitespace token carrying the line break at the end of a statement inside a nested code block, and roughly doubles to quadruples when that statement is a control-flow exit (break, continue, return, raise, throw, goto, exit) rather than an assignment or call. Ordinary statement lines inside a block give only a weak response (roughly 1.5-3.5, rising with nesting depth), a trailing blank line adds a further boost to non-jump lines, and top-level code at column 0, opening braces and running prose give no response.

The negative pole fires at the start of a prenominal modifier that stands between a quantifier and the head noun it modifies: an adjective, adverb or measure-word such as 'square' in '4,000 square feet', 'consecutive' in '42nd consecutive week', 'glorious' in 'five glorious victories', 'additional' in '30 additional years', or the ordinal/unit suffix token when it is fused to the numeral ('nd' in '42nd', '-b' in '137-bp'). It stays near zero when the quantifier is followed directly by its head noun ('three hours', 'five victories', '4,000 feet', '25 years'), when the same modifier follows an article or possessive ('the glorious victories', 'my glorious victories'), and on the head noun itself, which the neuron's positive pole picks up instead (0.5-0.9); strength is graded by how quantitative the determiner is (numerals 2.0-4.5 > few/many/some/dozens of/countless 1.1-1.6 > demonstratives ~1.0 > articles and possessives 0.1-0.5) and, within the construction, by modifier gradability (evaluative adjectives above classifying ones).

L15/N1572- is a verbatim-copy detector, not a topic or token detector: it fires on the tokens of a span that repeats, word for word, material already earlier in the same context - a duplicated credit/byline/song-list line, timestamp, URL, code identifier, heading, or a sentence the text has already used - and it sits at its floor on those very same tokens at their first occurrence (' Rebecca Lavelle' first mention 0.00 vs 1.87-2.28 once duplicated; 'Talking' 0.00 to 1.40-2.44; 'View this post' 0.01 to 1.31-1.94; 'Documentation' 0.00 to 2.41-2.97; ' Apr' 0.53 to 2.11-2.50) and on a parallel list whose items share the identical format but differ in content (three 'by <Name>' credits with three different names read 0.06, as do three 'Credits: Hosted by...' lines with distinct names). Within a copy the burst covers the whole copied span but peaks on its least predictable token (a name, capitalised identifier or number) and stays near zero on copied function words (the repeated ' by' of a byline reads 0.00), the level grows with the number of prior copies (2nd copy 0.3-2.4, 3rd-4th 1.2-2.5, then a plateau) and drops to 0.0-0.6 when the copy differs by one token at the measured position; an ordinary running-prose sentence repeated is the weak case (0.1-0.6).

The positive pole is a retrospective detector of author- and document-facing discourse: it fires on stretches where the writer's own voice is speaking (first person or possessive 'I/we/my' in a question or statement of the writer's situation, e.g. 'Q:\n\n... I was trying to...', 'I have a small...', 'We give...') or where a text or discussion is the thing being described or pointed at ('The article explains...', 'See also this article ... for more information'). The same content attributed to a third party leaves it near zero ('He was trying to shoot a group of people' 1.16 vs 'I was trying...' 3.07; 'She has a small dog' 0.21 vs 'I have a small dog' 1.29; 'The teacher explains' 0.03 vs 'The article explains' 0.98), as does ordinary third-person narration (<=0.1), and the pole's output direction promotes the vocabulary of explanation and discussion (explain, discuss, understand, inform, details).

L15/N3431- fires where the text specifies units of productive labour or of the compute that performs it: a counted or measured work-role (sixty engineers 1.75, two engineers 1.09, sixty developers 2.21, sixty labourers 2.00, hundreds of our nation's top scientists 1.64, upwards of 60 members of staff 3.86) or the machines doing that work (an 8-core processor 3.30, sixteen cores 3.30, the number of worker threads 3.79, sixty processors 2.47, sixty CPUs 2.05, sixty servers 1.61, sixty robots 1.13); the count/measure is what lifts it, since the same work-role without one stays low (engineers designed the bridge 0.07, the engineers at NASA 0.12). It stays near zero when the identical counting frame names performers, consumers, professional services or ordinary objects (sixty musicians/actors/dancers/tourists/lawyers/paintings 0.26-0.54, two musicians 0.39) and on figurative or performative work (the works of Shakespeare 0.02, she works as a musician 0.04), while a passage that already establishes a project's workforce, machinery or compute keeps it mildly elevated (0.7-1.5) on ordinary tokens there; the mechanism is retrospective.

A technical-notation register detector rather than a word detector: the pole is active on tokens inside source code and inside formal technical prose (methods sections, legal clauses, API documentation), where its peak lands on whichever nearby token carries the strongest surface marker of that register - a code keyword or operator ('import', '=', ':', '->', ' public', ' new'), a component of a dotted package, path or compound identifier (' org', '/libs', '-packages', 'Form'), or, in formal prose, the connective that introduces a technical term ('analysed by flow cytometry', 'processed using positron emission tomography', 'Clauses of the Constitution'). The same surface tokens inside narrative, conversational, poetic or plain journalistic prose sit near the floor (measured 0.02-0.40 against 0.6-2.8 on this scale), so the register of the surrounding passage, not the token identity, decides.

N4170− fires when the text refers to the older, incumbent or pre-digital form of a practice, technology or institution: either the modifier that labels it ('traditional', 'classic', 'classical', 'conventional', 'old', 'old-fashioned', 'analog', 'manual', 'film', 'previously', 'historically', 'used to') or the predicate that spells out how that older arrangement worked ('relies on', 'still based on', 'was delivered through'), as in 'replace the traditional cuff-based monitors', 'Updates used to be delivered through a separate software update app' or 'the disappearance of a linear path', whereas 'usual', 'customary', 'standard', 'modern', 'new', 'advanced' and 'newer' in the identical slots add nothing. It is retrospective and context-gated: the peak is on the modifier itself or on the preposition/copula of its phrase, and the same words stay low (0.1-1.2) unless the modern counterpart or the superseded category is already established in the preceding text (2.1-5.5 when it is: 'Advertising is cheap and precise. Traditional advertising is expensive' 2.98 vs the reversed order 0.70), while its output direction promotes exactly the old-world vocabulary ('paper', 'books', 'chalk', 'film', 'handwritten', 'analog', 'telephone', 'clergy', 'railroad') and suppresses modern-digital words ('internet', 'online', 'digital', 'smartphone', 'IoT', 'WiFi', 'Instagram', 'social media').

N4506+ fires when a specific referent has just been classified as a KIND - a nationality, ethnicity, religion, era, style, school, material or type ('German', 'Jewish', 'Catholic', 'Victorian', 'Gothic', 'Carolingian', 'socialist', 'rural', 'diesel', 'traditionalist') - and the clause then names the domain, respect or span in which that kind holds, with the peak on the preposition or possessive that links them and staying high over the scope phrase that follows ('English in his habits' 3.6, 'Italian in his tastes' 5.0, 'Swiss in its ownership' 4.3, 'Catholic in her sympathies' 4.1, 'French in character' 3.1, 'Gothic in its proportions' 2.8, 'Victorian in its proportions' 2.4, 'rural in its customs' 2.0). Both halves are needed: bare kind predication with no scope ('He was German.' 0.30, 'The building was Gothic.' 0.22, 'The wine was French.' 0.16), the identical scope frame filled with a scalar adjective ('illegible in its script' 0.22, 'cautious in its rhetoric' 0.15, 'happy in his drinking' 0.02), group-level generalizations ('Victorians are known for their morality' 0.06) and eventive reports of a referent's property ('their products reached forty markets' 0.16, 'its holdings were itemized' 0.03, 'its merchandise filled three storefronts' 0.02) all stay far below the 0.58 active threshold, and the response is retrospective - the peak sits on the linking token itself, rises over the scope phrase that has already been read, and zero-ablating the pole leaves next-token predictions essentially unchanged (next-token KL ~2e-4 in the scan's measurement).

Fires on a separator token (space, colon, dot, hyphen, parenthesis) or a digit immediately inside or just before a numeric literal such as a year, date, time, count, measurement, code constant, dimension, color value or contract/ID number, when that literal sits inside a longer formatted or structured span like code, logs, metadata headers or record tables. It reacts to the already-seen structured context plus the current delimiter or digit, not to prepare any specific upcoming token.

The positive pole fires on a token that is a word-piece rather than a word: a single alphabetic letter standing as a symbol - a variable ('Let q be', 'Suppose y equals'), an option/label/grade letter ('Option C was', 'Plan K', 'Grade A eggs', 'Class B', 'Figure C'), a judge's initial ('Smith, J.,'), a list or enumeration marker ('a, b, and c', 'a) b) c)'), or a letter being named ('the letter d') - at roughly 0.4-2.5 of max, and, more weakly and only when the piece is locally unpredicted, the first piece of a longer word that the tokenizer splits off ('Men|strual', ' rest|orative', ' ad|vertising', ' i|Frame', ' C|QL'). It stays near zero on complete multi-letter words even when they are surprising or collocation-breaking ('banana', 'reverence', 'zebra', 'wrestling', which drive the negative pole instead), on digits, punctuation, code and non-English text, and on single letters whose continuation is already fixed by a conventional term ('Section B describes', 'Vitamin B deficiency', 'A:' answer markers).

Retrospective: fires on a whole content word (noun, adjective, gerund, adverb, a sentence- or line-opening word, or the last piece that completes a tokenizer-split title word such as Cer|emony, Butter|flies, Sur|prising) whose identity the PRECEDING words did not predict, most strongly for abstract, institutional, collective or quantity/size words (knowledge, support, record, history, evidence, army, government, world, market, training, number, large, small) sitting right after an article, preposition, possessive or a sentence/line start; whether the word fits what comes after is irrelevant, so 'A large number of...', 'The world watched', 'the training program', 'after years of wrestling' and 'caused by number of' are all active. It stays near zero when the left context nearly forces the word ('for all of your support', 'Second World War', 'world record', 'basic training', 'stock market', 'in the history of'), on function words, pronouns, digits, punctuation, code keywords and the very first token of a text, and is usually weak (under ~0.3 of max) on a noun that follows an adjective and on mundane concrete nouns (chair, dog, car, park, shop, shirt, snow) even when they are surprising.

The negative pole fires at the point where a clause ties something to a hazard: the 'from'/'against' that introduces the source a defence predicate holds off ('protects the rider from injury', 'hardening federal buildings against threats', 'guards the village against floods', 'shields the heart from damage'), the 'by'/'with' that introduces the agent of a harmful state ('endangered by hunting', 'threatened by habitat loss', 'damaged by frost', 'breached by attackers', 'tampered with'), 'to' after 'vulnerable', and the negating element of an elaborated permission/prohibition notice ('may be reproduced ... without the prior written permission', the non-exclusive copyright grant). It stays near zero when the same prepositions carry a plain source, place or agent ('came from the city', 'a letter from my brother', 'played against the champions', 'leaned against the wall', 'monitors the network from the office', 'studied by researchers', 'designed by an architect', 'opened by the mayor') and on harm reported in the active voice with no such slot ('the storm damaged the roof', 'the frost killed the crops'); the hazard noun itself makes no difference ('against threats' and 'against weather' both peak at 2.68, 'damaged by the flood' and 'damaged by the workers' both at 0.67).

The pole fires while a passage is accumulating distinct national-scale referents - names of countries, of capitals or world cities that belong to different countries, national currencies, nationality adjectives, or international organisations - and it peaks on the comma, 'and', 'to' or other function word at the boundary where the next such referent is added (or on the first subword of that name), so the peak lands on the linker rather than on the name itself; strength rises with the number of distinct nations already on its left: one referent or a bare two-place relation stays at 0.1-0.75, two reach 1.1-1.9, three or four 1.7-3.7, and dense report, ranking or table lists 4.4-5.2. It stays at its floor when the enumeration remains inside a single nation (UK cities 0.74, US states 0.28, Canadian provinces and English counties 0.2-0.7, German Laender 0.14), when the listed items are not national-scale (animals 0.02, ordinary objects 0.07, car models 0.58, grape varieties 1.02, rivers 1.05), and on a single place name ('France is a country' 0.52) or a bare two-place relation ('between Germany and Brazil' 0.75); a list of personal names in the same enumerative frame sits in between (0.97-2.7) and never reaches the 3-5 band that country, world-city and international-organisation lists reach.

This pole is a retrospective detector for length/composition specifications of an account or identity credential field: it ramps up through clauses like 'password/PIN/username/passphrase must/should/needs/has (contain | have | be) (at least | exactly) N ...' and peaks on the quantity or complement token (eight, four, least, characters, number). Identical requirement wording with a non-credential subject (recipe, story, meal, contract, committee) evokes only weak activity, and the specific quantity word does not matter. Its output direction strongly suppresses name-related tokens, consistent with firing in credential-field contexts while suppressing name prediction; weak responses on other specifying complements (guilty, light, WHERE) are acknowledged offshoots.

The pole is a retrospective detector of words that name a relation of equality/equivalence or quantitative comparison: it takes its strongest scan values on ' relationship' (5.13, 'a curve-fit to determine the polynomial relationship'), ' equal' (4.53 in 'power-demanding equalisers', and roughly 0.3-1.0 of max in every sense, from 'equal to 44 per cent' and 'equal rights' to 'equalisers'), ' exponential' (4.13), ' equality' (3.53), the 'qu' piece of tokenizer-split inequity/inequitable (0.45-0.67 of max), and 0.1-0.6 of max on the relation nouns of quantitative analysis (correlation, relation, difference, comparison, similarity, metric, causal, correspond, proportional, dependence) plus ' unequal'. It is not a spelling or fairness detector: it stays at or below 0.1 of max on other 'equ' words (equipment, equation, equilibrium, adequate, sequel), on 'qu' inside non-equ words ('earthquake' 0.09, 'vanquished' 0.00), on the fairness/justice lexicon (fair, fairness, justice, discrimination, bias, parity), on generic comparison words (link, gap, pattern), on ' independence' in its political/personal sense ('financial independence' 0.00 against 2.48 for statistical independence assumptions), and on ' equality' as the head of a social-identity compound (gender/racial/marital/gay equality 0.02-0.4 of max against 0.4-1.0 for the bare noun); within-word variation remains only partly explained ('created equal' 0.00), with unexplained leftovers on evolutionary/ecological and the keep/kept/holding tokens.

Qwen2.5-0.5B L16/N1584- fires on the lecture/talk schema: a scheduled occasion at which someone speaks to an audience. It peaks on the word that names such an occasion (lecture, talk, keynote, seminar, symposium, colloquium, webinar, presentation, speech, sermon, briefing, conference, session, classroom), on the person who speaks at or attends one (speaker, presenter, lecturer, panelist, attendee, participant), and on the participation verbs attend / speak at / present at / headline when their object is such an occasion; it fires for unseen synonyms, in past, scheduled and announcement frames, and in other languages (French conference 3.85, Chinese 讲座 3.66 and 演讲 2.57). It stays below the activity line for other kinds of scheduled happening (party, wedding, funeral, protest, rally, election, exam, interview, exhibition, screening, recital, play, gig; a bare 'concert' is the one partial exception I could not explain), for venue and equipment words (auditorium, podium, microphone), and for non-talk senses of its words (the speaker on my phone, the speaker of the parliament, the class struggle, talk about the budget, attend to a patient).

Fires on a token whose text begins with the letter sequence 'str' (any case, with or without a leading space or hyphen), strongest (about 0.5-1.0 of max) when that token is a bare sub-word fragment such as 'str', ' Str', 'Str', '-str', ' strat', ' stre' that opens a longer word or name (stratospheric, Stringer, Stroud, Lindström, strait, single-stranded, stratification); whole-word 'str' tokens are weaker (' string', ' strategic', ' strict', ' stretch' about 0.1-0.6, depending on context), very common whole words (' strong', ' street', ' structure') are near zero, and tokens without the 'str' onset (' St', 'thr', ' D') are inactive. It is retrospective: the activation reads the current token's spelling, with little dependence on earlier context, and the Jacobian lens (kurtosis 3.2) promotes no coherent next-token set.

The pole fires on the linking or metalinguistic token that introduces a specific named expression: inside Title-Case (or quoted/italicised) work titles and name phrases it peaks on the lowercase connective (' of' in "The Picture of the Day", ' a' in "To Kill a Mockingbird", ' to' in "A Farewell to Arms", ' on' in "Attack on Titan"), and in term/label constructions it peaks on the word or field label that introduces the expression (' term', ' word', ' phrase', 'Terms like', 'Quote:', 'Keywords:', 'See also', 'abstract:'). The same words in ordinary lower-case prose, as isolated tokens, or in non-naming headings such as 'Notes:'/'Warning:' stay near zero, so the trigger is the name/term-mention frame rather than token identity.

This pole fires on a prenominal modifier that identifies which instance, value or version of the head noun is meant - the determinative adjectives certain, specific, particular, given, specified, designated, predetermined, preset, predefined, fixed, default, desired, intended, requested, chosen, selected, arbitrary, same, different, respective - and not on the article, on demonstratives/quantifiers/ordinals (every 0.07, each 0.07, first 0.07, only 0.07, this 0.72, that 1.23, against 4.84 for 'a certain' in the same frame) or on ordinary descriptive adjectives in the identical slot (a large number 0.18, a blue car 0.02, a central angle 0.06, a long letter 0.06). It tracks that sense rather than the surface word or what follows it: 'a certain amount of time' peaks 9.48 on ' certain' but 'I am certain the ...' only 0.23, 'a fixed price' 2.55 but 'they fixed a price' 0.41, 'a given day' 5.32 but 'given the circumstances' 0.25, the negated 'unspecified' keeps only half (2.34 against 5.06), the token after the modifier is always at the floor (amount 0.00, direction 0.00, genre 0.00), and the negative pole never leaves zero, so the pole marks the identifying modifier itself and nothing downstream.

The negative pole is a ball-game-play detector: it fires on passages where a ball or puck is being played in a sporting contest - kicked, thrown, passed, hit, shot, crossed, cleared, headed, putted or carried into or past a target, or to a teammate - and on the scoring plays, points, records and match statistics that report such play, in English or Chinese. Its activity spreads over the whole passage (most input attribution sits more than 16 tokens back, mean distance 46) and peaks on whichever token carries the play or the statistic ('-point' in '800 3-pointers', 'tries' in a try-scoring line, ' hit' in 'he hit .200', 'passing' in '577 passing yards', the 'the'/' into' of 'crossed the ball into the box'), while ball-less sport (400 m running, swimming, chess, esports), ball-sport administration and business news (fixtures, transfers, kit), ordinary motion of non-ball objects and non-sporting numbers stay near zero; outside a formal game it still fires on the same ball-propulsion schema ('kicked the ball into the hedge' 6.3 vs 'kicked the stone into the hedge' 1.2).

The negative pole responds to a field of a biology/medicine literature record, peaking on the separator or whitespace that opens its next field - the ':' in 'Magn Reson Med. 2019;81[:]2551-2565', the space before the pages when the same citation is written out as prose ('...in Magnetic Resonance in Medicine in 2019, volume 81, pages[ ]2551'), the space after '=' in an abstract's statistics ('95% CI =[ ]2.35-15.88'), and the ') (' that closes a long typed parameter list and opens the result list of a signature. Identically formatted citations carrying a physics/engineering/computing venue ('Phys Rev B. 2019;81:2551-2565', 'Adv Neural Inf Process Syst. 2017;30:5998-6008'), the same numbers in running prose, and ordinary narrative text stay near zero.

Fires when the text conventionally designates something — an individual, place, kind or title is said to be called / known as / termed / described as / dubbed / nicknamed / referred to as ['the'] Y (Chinese 被称为 / 称为 / 俗称) — with the peak on the naming predicate (' called', ' known', '被称为') and/or on the determiner that opens the designation (' the Y'). It stays near zero on the phone/summon sense of 'call', on one-off naming of a particular person, on plain taxonomic labelling of an ordinary object ('My friend is called John', 'The teacher called the student a genius', 'The student was called a genius', 'The tool is called a hammer', 'The function is called the sigmoid function' — all ≤ 0.15 of the scan max), and on ordinary declaratives or plain copulas with no naming predicate; inside the frame the strength is graded, with habitual adverbs, definite designations and place/kind subjects reaching 0.5-1.4x the scan max.

Fires retrospectively on predicate verbs and event tokens (such as 'runs', 'opened', 'returns', 'works', 'went', 'rushed', 'flooded') when the grammatical subject is inanimate, computational, or non-agentive, rather than an animate agent. It distinguishes non-agentive operations, inchoative transitions, and operational execution from intentional human or animal actions.

The negative pole fires when a comparative is used in a definite or clause-initial frame in a short clause: 'the more/less + ADJECTIVE' (peaks on 'more'/'less' and on the adjective after it, e.g. 'The more expensive model is better.', 'The more detailed analysis revealed the problem.'), the 'the X-er, the Y-er' correlative ('The more you practice, the better you get.', 'The bigger the better.'), the sentence-initial attributive 'the ADJ-er + noun' (strongest for bigger/stronger/larger/higher/faster/lighter/longer/louder/better; cheaper/lower/older/taller/sooner are near-threshold), and the appositive 'NP, on the other hand, VP' pivot (peak on 'other'); a short adverbial lead-in ('In practice, the more detailed analysis...') preserves firing, a subject-verb lead-in does not. It is inactive (below 0.25 x max) for predicative 'X is ADJ-er than Y' with an explicit than-target, quantity 'more/less + plural noun', superlatives (most/best/least), bare intensifiers (very/extremely), isolated non-English comparative markers (更/más/plus), contracted 'what's more', mid-clause 'the more ADJ' after a subject-verb, and sentence-initial adverbial 'On the other hand, ...'; the two strongest unmatched scan peaks ('but' 5.47 after 'Like flares', ')' 4.18 after a statistical parenthetical) need their full multi-sentence contexts and are acknowledged leftovers.

L16/N4681+ fires on the interior of a word the tokenizer has had to spell out in pieces, when that word is a name, a Latin/Greek technical term or a code identifier rather than ordinary English vocabulary: the current token has no leading space and continues the previous token's word, and the peak sits on the fragment that carries the word's distinctive spelling ('opt' in Hymenoptera 2.8, 'onal' in clonal 2.5, 'inement' in bx_refinement 2.4, 'Parent' in m_pParentNode 1.5, 'ological' in Histological 2.0, the '9' of x509 3.0). Strength is graded by how name-like or technical the word is - capitalised name forms fire 1.3-2x the same word in lowercase ('Histological' 2.01 vs 'histological' 1.29, 'Hymenopteran' 2.76 vs 'hymenopteran' 1.40) - and it falls to the floor on any token that starts a word (the identical string: ' Instance' 0.06 vs 'Instance' 1.55), on pieces of ordinary vocabulary and of compounds of ordinary English words (the 'ization' of institutionalization 0.32, the 'Timeout' of RequestTimeout 0.60, the 'conf' of nginx.conf (peak 0.31)), and on technical terms that the tokenizer splits into ordinary fragments inside plain lowercase prose (the 'alan' of acanthocephalan 0.19).

The negative pole fires at the stem/suffix boundary of a real, non-nonsense multi-token word: it peaks on the word-internal fragment token immediately before the word's final piece ('ange' in hydr|ange|a, 'hec' in Semnopit|hec|us, 'д' in сопрово|д|ение, 'h' in Trabal|h|adores), fires more weakly on earlier fragments near the word's end, and is silent on the word-final token itself, on single-token and two-piece words, on fragments followed by stem material, and on nonsense words or code. Its write promotes a broad class of word-final suffix tokens ('ers', 'ation', 'us', 'ia', 'es', 'as') rather than committing to one particular ending, marking the point in a word where an ending is due.

The pole fires on the token that carries a stored, non-compositional string rather than a composed phrase: the opening word-piece of a person or organisation name (' McC' in John McCracken, ' Car' in David Carlucci, ' Co' in Peter Cooley, ' Writers' plus its possessive apostrophe in "Baseball Writers' Association of America"), a domain or file-path fragment ('bo' in boingboing.net, '.do' in docs.doctrine-project.org), or a fixed boilerplate/technical phrase (' entry' in 'any responses to this entry', ' Application' in 'Japanese Patent Application'), often on two or three consecutive tokens of the same string. Strength tracks how firmly the string is stored -- 'Baseball Writers'' 5.7 > 'Football Writers'' 2.5 > 'Martian Writers'' 0.35, 'Peter Cooley' 2.1 > 'Peter Nordland' 0.5 -- while the same surface token inside composed or lower-case prose ('writers'' association', 'the senator John', 'John Smith') stays at the ~0.2 baseline; the numerous weak 0.4-0.9 firings on common words (' get', ' just', ' the', ' if') sit in the opposite SwiGLU sign regime (gate negative, up positive) and are a different, diffuse mechanism.

This pole fires retrospectively when the current token completes a conventional, stereotyped multi-token construction: an idiom or collocation (pinch/bag of salt, at sea), a memorized proper name or fact (Neil after Moon-and, Seine, sea level in the boiling-point sentence), or a boilerplate measure, legal, or technical slot (greater-than five, times-a-day, from-9-a.m.-to, raised interest, negative charge, pleaded not guilty), with strength scaling with canonicality (salt 7.7-13.6 after of-phrases vs pepper 0.3-0.8; runs 0.29 vs eats 0.06). The identical surface token in a novel or compositional frame stays near silent (guilty 0.50 vs 0.00, charge 0.64 vs 0.01, Neil 1.20 with Apollo context vs 0.04 without), so the claim beats the token-identity confound (R2 82%). The effect is detection of the just-completed frame, not preparation of the next token: the Jacobian lens is Gaussian noise (kurtosis 3.3) whose promoted tokens never follow the peaks, and swapping the word after the peak (Neil Armstrong/ate, sea level/food, hall fell silent/apart) leaves the peak unchanged.

Retrospective detector for the onset of reported/quoted material in a reportive frame: activation climbs through the attribution clause ('she said,', 'greeted her with', 'I thought:'), peaks on the opening quotation mark that follows it (' "', ' “', ' ‘'), stays elevated across the quoted words, and collapses at the closing quote; the frame carries most of the response (deleting the two quote glyphs costs only ~0.12 of max, and bare quoted dialogue lines still give ~0.5), while the same string in a machine-log frame, config/identifier string literals (JSON keys, #include headers), line-initial quotes after a newline, and impersonal news-register scare quotes sit near zero, and a moderate secondary trigger (~0.25-0.4 of max) fires on numerals ('4 years ago', '2019', '100%') and a few technical-term onsets (' mult'ithreading, ' Bio'hazard) in running prose. The response is gated by document register rather than context length (a 16-token prompt reaches 0.98 of scan max; dialogue-dense or voiced-personal documents lift the whole span with median up to ~0.6 of max, and the same quoted tail gains ~+0.33 of max after a personal-narrative vs technical prefix); the Jacobian promoted list is incoherent (kurtosis 4.6 but 10% lens agreement, CJK/formatting tokens with no overlap with quoted-speech continuations), so this is not lookahead for specific quoted tokens, and the negative pole owns the opposite material - the author's own interpolated voice in parenthetical asides ('(Nooo kidding, John!)', ', of all places,').

Fires on the non-final digits of a large numeral written with a thousands separator in running prose (prices, populations, square footage, viewer counts), peaking on the 1st and 2nd digit after the ',' (any digit value, not just '0'; weaker with '.'), and staying near zero on the last digit of a group, on spelled-out numbers ('seven thousand', '$25 million'), and on years and other short numbers. Weaker secondary triggers are the pandoc citation opener '[@' (but not '[#', '[$' or '(@'), 'World/world' in set phrases ('Book of World Records', "the world's first"), and the article ' a' right after a preposition that opens a modified noun phrase ('by a combined', 'in a statistical tie'; ' the' there gives about half as much); preceding news-style prose roughly doubles the response compared with chit-chat or code context.

Fires on a transitive verb (or the perfect auxiliary 'have/has' right before it) whose direct object has already been supplied to its left, so no object is expected after it: the verb of an object-gap relative clause with or without 'that' ('the table I found', 'the house Jack built', 'the option people have had', 'everything you need'), or a participle whose subject is its patient ('a method has been developed', 'has been known'). It stays near zero on the same verb when an agentive subject precedes it and an object is still to come ('I found the table', 'engineers have developed a system', 'when it released the cables'); it reads only left context, and is strongest when the fronted head is an inanimate thing rather than a person.

In prose that reports experimental or debugging results, fires on the last token of a clause's subject (head noun, closing ',' or ')' of an appositive or relative clause, or a pre-verbal 'also'/'it'), when that subject names a manipulation, agent or tested condition (gene knock-out, drug treatment, inhibitor, oligomers, 'when I comment it out') and the predicate about to follow will report its observed effect. It is strongest when a negative or contrastive outcome is set up ('None of the ...', 'however', '... did not'), and weak or absent when the same noun is an object or a procedural or descriptive mention ('we stored the oligomers', 'read-out of the gene') or appears in non-experimental narrative.

The pole responds primarily to typographic layout rather than to content: it fires hardest on the token that closes or terminates a markup element (‘</’, ‘ </’, ‘></’, ‘>\n’, ‘">\r\n’) and on the capitalised first word of a paragraph opened by a blank line — headings and section starts such as ‘Copy’, ‘Two’, ‘Long’, ‘Over’, ‘Print’, ‘Execute’ (8% of paragraph-initial capitals reach the protocol's active threshold, versus 2% of all tokens). Running lowercase prose and sub-word continuations stay near zero, and the response falls by roughly two thirds when the same heading word is lowercased or pulled into the running line; headings whose opener is not a label-like word (‘Move’) fire far less, a lexical residual the layout account does not explain.

The negative pole fires on the token that closes a slot in laid-out text - the ':' ending an aligned 'Label:' field, the final character of a padded identifier, citation, docket number or filename, the tail of a Markdown underline or ASCII rule, a table cell, or a sentence-final period before a wide gap - i.e. on the token immediately before a whitespace-only token (padding spaces or a blank line), with the peak on that closing token rather than on the whitespace. It requires the layout to be established earlier in the document: the same words with single spaces between fields stay near baseline (0.44 of 11.56), a lone padded line reaches only 0.09, and one earlier padded line lifts the next field's ':' from 0.09 to 4.53; its output direction promotes exactly those padding whitespace tokens, but the zero-ablation KL averaged over the base prompts is 3.1e-4, below the lookahead threshold, because the pole is active on fewer than 0.1% of scan tokens, so the mechanism is claimed retrospective.

The positive pole fires when text fixes a quantity to a scale: it peaks on the token that introduces the value (the space or delimiter before the number in 'p < 0.001', 'BMI > 30', '0.4 to 0.9', '% 74,1 2.927', '$50 $40', or a JSON/XML field) and on the bound or degree word that sets such a value ('below', 'above', 'within', 'exceeding', 'ranging from ... to', 'the point of'), and it is strongest in documents that enumerate many such values (election-result tables 5.5-6.6 of the 6.57 scan max, price lists 5.7, statistics-heavy abstracts 4.2-4.5, dimension-laden layout code 3.3-3.5), whereas a quantity merely mentioned in narrative prose does not fire it ('There were 12 apples' 0.32, 'born in 1987' 0.16) and neither does ordinary descriptive or inceptive prose ('the beginning of the story' 0.06, 'She began to read the whole book' 0.02). The same neuron's negative pole, which fires on totality words quantifying a consumed mass ('all' -3.4, 'whole' -2.7, 'entire' -4.4), is the other end of one axis - a determinate value or bound on a scale versus the whole amount - and the pole is retrospective (zero-ablation KL 1.5e-4 on the top prompts, is_lookahead False; the Jacobian lens's begin/start token list does not match what follows the peaks, which is a numeral or the token introducing one).

L17/N2593+ fires on the connector that closes a formally-named designation, above all the ' of' (and its equivalents ' van'/' de'/' la') that attaches a named legal or official instrument to its qualifier: 'the Statute of limitations' 10.7, 'the Ordinance of 1787' 12.0, 'the Decree of the committee' 10.1, 'the Act of God' 12.9, 'the Civil Rights Act of 1964' 11.0, 'the Treaty of Paris' 7.1, 'Apache License, Version 2.0' 6.6, weakening through other title-cased names (Council/Committee/Court/House/Order/Medal/League/Battle/Gulf/Revolution, 1.7-5.0) and through the 2-3 band of ' of' inside institutional and encyclopedic titles ('Court of Appeals', 'Medal of Honor', 'Forest of Dean'). It is near zero on the same connector after abstract, mass, partitive or generic-role nouns ('the idea of justice' 0.0, 'the use of force' 0.0, 'the regulation of the market' 0.04, 'the Ministry of Defence' 0.25, 'the University of Oxford' 0.7), on the lowercase common-noun use of an instrument word ('the act of God' 1.4 vs 'the Act of God' 12.9), on every other preposition after the same nouns ('the Statute on limitations' 0.9, 'the Decree by the committee' 1.8) and on bare dates with no designation ('He graduated from college in 1998' 0.4). The response reads only words already present - a year or a common noun after the same ' of' leaves it bit-identical ('the Ordinance of 1787' 11.99 = 'the Ordinance of the committee' 11.99) - while its output direction promotes the calendar months (13 of its top-13 raw-unembedding promotions, 9 of the top-10 Jacobian-lens tokens), so it writes a date bias rather than predicting a specific upcoming token, and the protocol's lookahead probe returns retrospective.

Lexical detector that fires on the token itself for spatial-orientation/geometric-axis adjectives (' vertical', ' horizontal', ' perpendicular', ' parallel', ' vertically', ' flat', 'ob|lique') and on the word-initial prefix piece ' hyper' (hyperlinks, hyperactive, hyperchromatic, hyperparathyroidism), with weaker firing on ' flex' (flexor), ' virtual' and the ':\n' after an 'address'/'author' key in arXiv-style YAML metadata; near-orientation synonyms (' upright', ' diagonal', ' cross') and the following noun stay near zero.

The positive pole fires on the possessive 'at' phrase of terms and prerogative - 'at' + your/its/their + (own/sole) + a noun naming what is left to a party or at stake for it ('at your option' 14.5, 'at its sole discretion' 25.7, 'at their option' 16.2, 'at your own risk' 23.3, 'at your earliest convenience' 8.1, and the modal permission 'you may use the software at your home' 15.1) - and on the copyright-licence formula 'Use of this/these <thing> is ...' ('Use of this source code is governed by ...' 11.3). It peaks on the possessive determiner itself or on the 'at' immediately before it and its output finishes the phrase ('at'->'your', 'your'->'own', 'its'->'sole'; ablating it shifts probability onto ' own', ' option', ' risk', ' sole'), while it stays near zero on locative or temporal 'at' without a possessive ('at the station' 0.4, 'at 37 C' 0.0, 'at noon' 0.0, 'at 3 percent' 1.3, 'at 60 mph' 0.1), on 'at + possessive' inside plain event narration ('we stayed at your house' 0.2, 'she looked at your picture' 0.3, 'the parties met at their office' 1.0), on a third-person possessive in a stative location ('the book is at his home' 1.1, 'at its home' 0.4, 'at the home' 0.2), and on licence wording outside those formulae ('Permission is hereby granted' 0.7, 'IN NO EVENT SHALL' 0.4, 'This software is licensed under' 0.5, 'You may not use this file except in compliance' 2.7).

L17/N3698+ fires on the tokens that carry the non-linguistic payload of machine-formatted text: digits inside multi-digit numeric literals (the '0' of port 5000, of 62.5%, of -Xmx1024m), the '%' of a printf-style format verb, and the internal fragments or punctuation of identifiers, URLs and config strings (the 'Base' of DefaultBaseURI, '=-' in jvmargs=-Xmx1024m, '[it' in properties[it], 'Name' of sServerName). The same digits, percents and fragments embedded in ordinary narrative prose ('the port was 5000' after a descriptive sentence, '100 % of the students', 'ten point five percent') leave it at or below 0.5 of its 3.98 max, so the pole reads the code/quantitative register built up over the preceding tens of tokens rather than the token identity alone.

Fires on the word 'single' itself (any case, including the subword 'ingle' in camelCase 'singleLine') when it is used in its plain counting/category sense of 'exactly one unit' or 'one-unit kind' (single-photon, single-center, a single game, single room/ticket, single mother, 'I am single'), at roughly 0.6-1.0 of max; other multiplicity words fire much more weakly (double ~0.35-0.45, multi/dual/sole/mon(o)/one ~0.1-0.3, return/twin/great ~0). The pole is strongly suppressed (<~0.25 of max) when 'single' is the emphatic polarity intensifier after 'every', 'not a', 'not one', 'without a' or 'just a', or the music-release noun after 'released', 'new', 'latest', 'first' or 'lead'; plain predicate negation ('I am not single') does not suppress it, and tokens after 'single' are inactive.

Fires on tokens in computer/software/web text - code and command lines, URLs and file paths, config/log/format strings, API doc comments, and interface text or page chrome addressed to the user (open/click/type/press with a digital object such as file, folder, app, page, menu, settings, button; 'leave a comment', 'sign in to continue', '1,325 shares') - peaking on the digital artifact's name or on the technical literal (an identifier or CamelCase piece, UI label, flag, path component, version or id number). It stays near zero in narrative, news, academic and general expository prose, including prose that describes computing systems abstractly (compilers, databases, algorithms), and on physical objects even inside the same imperative frames (door, box, garden, boat).

The positive pole encodes effortful striving: it fires on the verbs that name the act of trying to reach a goal (try/tries/tried/trying 9.5-16.3, strive/strove 10.0-12.5, struggle 5.0, fought 6.3, battle 2.3, work/works/working/worked 4.3-7.4, aim 6.4, attempt 3.9, endeavour 3.6, toil 6.2, labour 1.7-3.0, slog 1.2, compete 3.9, on a 16.8 peak) and on the degree words that grade that effort ('hard' 9.6 right after 'try', 'hardest' 10.1, 'very' 4.0, 'really' 4.7), while staying near baseline on verbs that take the identical 'to + infinitive' complement but express intention, permission or success (want 0.45, need 0.23, plan 0.07-0.31, decide 0.08, agree 1.16, promise 0.21, refuse 0.07-0.26, seem 0.12-0.20, begin 0.00, manage 0.06), on effort nouns ('The attempt failed' 0.03, 'His effort' 0.03, 'great effort' 0.05) and on 'hard/very/extremely' outside an effort frame ('a hard problem' 0.19, 'hard to say' 0.31, 'extremely cold' 0.42, 'hit the ball hard' 0.00). Its output direction writes exactly those effort intensifiers forward (' hard' +2.4, 'hardest' +2.2, 'very' +1.9, 'harder' +1.9, 'really' +2.1, 'exceptionally' +1.9 logits at the peaks, measured by zero-ablating the pole) while the negative pole never exceeds 0.4 on the same strings, so it is a detector of effort rather than one end of a dial; leftovers it does not explain: possessives after 'try' split oddly ('try our/my best' 14.8/15.5 vs 'try his/their best' 2.0/4.4) and exertion verbs that do not take a to-infinitive goal stay low (persist 0.00, grind 0.02, push 0.71, achieve 0.63, commit 0.31).

In Java/C++/JS-like source, this pole fires on the token opening an integer-count value slot: the '=' of a declaration/assignment whose declared type is an integer type (int, unsigned int) or whose untyped var/bare target is a cardinal count/index noun (total, count/counter, numberOfItems, currentpage), and the 'return' of a predicate-guarded early exit (if-contains/equals ... return true/false) in a boolean- or int-returning method. It stays near zero when the slot's type is floating-point or text/object (double, float, float64, String, Object, collections), when the identifier denotes a non-count aggregate, ratio, duration or generic computed result (average, ratio in a typed declaration, elapsedMillis, Go result float64, computed tax/rate), on non-code '=' analogues (JSON colon values, SQL WHERE, shell assignments, prose 'Let x =', Python object bindings, compound '+=') and on unguarded bare returns (int getter, computed-double return).
